The strongest hunters develop a personal form that no school taught them, a breathing technique unique to how they body and will work together.

lore.name: Cedars, Pines and Bamboo
lore.info: Cedars, pines and bamboo are the trees of the isles. Black cedars clothe the Kurosugi Range and the hidden valleys of its villages, and woodcutters fell them and float the logs down to the plain. The Ayakashi Wood is cedar and camphor, some trees older than the empire, and loggers who push into it for the capital's lumber merchants sleep close to their fires. Pines line the post road; along Pine Avenue they are so old their split trunks are propped up with poles. Bamboo grows in dense groves that knock and whisper in the wind, and gatherers cut the shoots in spring. A tree with a straw rope tied around it belongs to a kami and is never cut, and woodcutters leave an offering before felling any tree old enough to have a name. In the Ashfall Blight only dead white trunks stand, and nothing has grown there since the war.

lore.name: Children and Upbringing
lore.info: Children in the isles start working as soon as they can carry something. Farm children fetch water, scare birds from the paddies and walk the dikes behind their parents; in the woodcutters' hamlets they carry water between the sheds; miners' children haul ore baskets beside their mothers. A child's training follows the family trade: a smith's son works the bellows, a Hiwada child is in the saddle almost as soon as it can sit, and Kagegi children are throwing blades at posts in the cedar clearings while other children learn their letters. Children orphaned by demon raids in the north are taken in at the Orphans' Lodge below Hinode Fortress and trained as hunters once they are old enough. Small children are dressed in bright colours and carried to the shrine to be shown to the local kami, and their names are entered in the village or temple register so the magistrate knows how many mouths a village feeds. Mothers and grandmothers raise the little ones, and the trades take over the rest.

lore.name: Children's Proverbs
lore.info: The isles teach wisdom to children through proverbs and stories: 'The sword that draws first is drawn last'—honour lies in restraint. 'The river runs to the sea, never backward'—accept what is given, work with what you have. 'The mountain does not bend to the wind'—holding firm has its own strength. 'The rice plant bows low with a full head'—wisdom is humble. 'The fox remembers what the dog forgets'—cunning lasts when strength fades. 'The night is darkest before the dawn'—despair is often the test before salvation. These proverbs are taught by mothers and grandmothers, reinforced by teachers and masters, and lived by people trying to understand their lives.

lore.name: Clothing and Dress
lore.info: Clothing in the isles tells a stranger most of what they need to know. Everyone wears the kimono in some form, wrapped left over right and tied with a sash, and a plain one in an ordinary colour costs about 6 Mon at any outfitter and lets its wearer vanish in a crowd. Working people hitch up their hems and tie back their sleeves with a cord; travellers add a deep straw hat and straw sandals that wear through every few days. Colour and crest mark allegiance: Shogunate officials in grey, Warden riders in blue, guild clerks in dark blue coats, Bureau students in white, Veil officers in black coats, breath hunters in dark uniforms under patterned haori, and samurai in their house's crest. Summer brings bright cotton yukata for festivals, and the north lives in seal fur, without which nobody crosses the Reach in winter. White is worn by mourners and by the dead. A long foreign wool coat with brass buttons, about 10 Mon at an outfitter, marks a sailor who has served on foreign ships.

lore.name: Coaches and Ferries
lore.info: A coach travels the post road every few days, pulled by strong horses and carrying goods and passengers for hire. A coach is safer than riding alone and slower than riding hard; a seat from one district's town to the next costs about twelve Mon, more for a long stage or a rich-looking traveller. Ferries cross the two straits: the Ember Strait between the Fifty Stations Road and Tetsuyama, and the White Strait between the Kurosugi Range and the Hyoga Reach. A crossing costs about thirty Mon, because a strait is harder than a stage. Both ferries run when the weather permits and the masters say the sea is calm. Ferries sometimes take three days to cross or miss a journey entirely when the wind rises.

lore.name: Courtship and Romance
lore.info: Romance in the isles follows rules set by families and society: a young person of marriage age is introduced to prospects by family or matchmaker. Meetings are formal, supervised, and governed by protocol. A courtship begins in secret touches and meaningful looks; a declaration of love is a serious matter that implies intent to marry. A samurai may have a courtship carried on for years; a merchant may marry quickly once terms are agreed. Unmarried lovers meeting secretly are treated with sympathy by ordinary folk but harshly by families protecting their honour and their daughter's prospects. A love that crosses house boundaries must be extraordinary to survive.

lore.name: Crafting in the Isles
lore.info: Four crafts make things in the isles. Smiths forge blades, spears and lacquered armour at a forge or anvil (Forging). Apothecaries make salves, tonics and poisons at a still or in a kitchen (Medicine). Artificers build traps, locks and mechanisms at a workbench (Artifice). Shrine scribes write talismans and ward-charms at a shrine or writing desk (Warding). Work is graded plain, Fine, Superior, Master-made and Named; a Named piece is known by its name across the isles. Master-made and Named work is done only at the great stations: Forging: Forge Guild Hall, Hibana, The Workshop; Medicine: Hayate Ridge Village; Artifice: Mask-Maker's Workshop; Warding: Bureau of Yin and Yang, Crater Rim Shrine. No bench makes a soul-blade: those wake, or are forged from living souls in secret, and that is another story.

lore.name: Curses, Curse Wells and the Economy of Grudge
lore.info: A curse is a grudge given weight and shape, binding itself to a person or object and refusing to let go. Curses cannot be removed but only managed, passed on, or soured into power. Ashfall Blight is full of curse wells—places where grudges were so deep and old that they pooled in the earth and became physical. The Grudge Well Sorcerers harvest these wells' power and sell cursed objects through Saikai's darker merchants, making fortunes by binding curses into relics. A cursed relic might grant power, or it might drain its owner's life slowly; the curse's nature is written in how it hungers. The strongest curses develop will and memory; some ancient curses have been passed through a hundred owners and have grown into beings that wear their hosts like clothes. A curse-bearer who masters their curse learns to make it an weapon rather than a wound.

lore.name: Demon-Slayer's Sunlight and Sun-Steel
lore.info: Sun-steel is forged at the Sun-Steel Forge in Hinode Fortress, whose fire is lit only at dawn, by a process that captures sunlight in the metal, making blades that demons cannot stand near without burning. A sun-steel blade is painful to hold for most people after a while; only the breath hunters and a few devoted others can wield them for long. The hunters say the best blades are struck in the first light of the year's longest days; all of them are deadly to demons. The Breath Hunters of Hinode Hold use sun-steel nearly exclusively, and their battles with the Northern Court's demons are a clash of their burning light against the demons' living shadow. Demons that die to sun-steel do not return, which is why the demons fear it most of all.

lore.name: Demons of the Northern Court
lore.info: The demons of the Northern Court come from the far north, beyond the Long Night Wall, where the demon lord keeps a palace of black ice and the night lasts most of the year. The south calls him the Lord of the Long Night; no living southerner has seen him. Demons are not yokai and not spirits: they are hunger with bodies of shadow, and most of them cannot endure sunlight or sun-steel. They climb by strength: common demons are clever, small things; ranked demons are persons with will and cunning; demon nobles rule hosts of the lesser; three eldest serve the lord himself, older than the empire's walls. On the long winter nights the demons come south to hunt, and the Breath Hunters of Hinode call those seasons the Demon Nights. A demon slain by sun-steel or the dawn does not return, which is why the hunters fight in the light whenever they can.

lore.name: District: Ashfall Blight
lore.info: Ashfall Blight is a district of the Asagiri Isles. The southwest plain where the last great war was fought and never quite ended: grey ash for soil, broken banners, craters, dead orchards, and wells that brim with curse instead of water. Curse-bearers walk here because nothing else will have them, and the vow temples on its low hills take oaths that bind for life. Grudges outlast the dead in the Blight. Its town is Haibara; its other places: Grudge Well Sanctum, Curse-Hunters' Chapterhouse, The Ash Plain, Ruins of the Old Capital, Haibara Ash Market, Weeping Cedar, Bone Gully, Ash Crow Roost, Inugami Kennels, Grey Pilgrims' Road, Sunken Well Village, Moth Dell. By land it joins Fifty Stations Road, Saikai Free Port.

lore.name: District: Ayakashi Wood
lore.info: Ayakashi Wood is a district of the Asagiri Isles. An ancient forest north of the lake that rearranges its paths when it is displeased: twisting cedars and camphor trees, fox shrines in every hollow, fox-fire on the paths at dusk, and Tengu Peak rising out of the canopy. The yokai courts keep their own law here, and half-yokai who belong nowhere else find a refuge in its depths. Humans who keep their manners usually come out again. Its town is Kitsunebi Crossing; its other places: Halls of the Nine-Tailed Lady, Tengu Peak, Two-Blooded Refuge, Kodama Grove, Spider Woman's House, Tanuki Market, Loggers' Camp, Crow Tengu Nests, Foxfire Marsh, Shrine of the Fallen Feather, Whispering Bamboo, Kitsune Shrine Road. By land it joins Hinode Hold, Kurosugi Range, Seimei Bureau.

lore.name: District: Fifty Stations Road
lore.info: Fifty Stations Road is a district of the Asagiri Isles. The great highway from Saikai's east gate along the edge of the Blight, past the capital and on to the marsh coast: post stations a day apart, inns with paper lanterns, tea houses, toll barriers that check papers and station, and the bandits who watch the barriers from the hills. Every traveller in the isles passes along it; at the Oiwake crossroads the road north climbs to the capital and the road south runs down to Ember Strait. Its town is Oiwake Station; its other places: Road Commissioner's Office, Seventh Station Inn, Cedar Pass Barrier, Red Lantern Roost, Duelists' Teahouse, Pine Avenue, River Ferry Crossing, Ghost Pine Hill, Bandits' Bridge, Wayside Jizo Shrine, Rice-Cake Peddlers' Rest, Porters' Lodge. By land it joins Ashfall Blight, Mistmarsh Coast, Miyako Plain, Saikai Free Port; by sea Tetsuyama (across Ember Strait).

lore.name: District: Hinode Hold
lore.info: Hinode Hold is a district of the Asagiri Isles. The snowbound north of the main island, its highest peaks facing the sunrise, crowned by the breath hunters' fortress. Below it the night valleys hold demon nests that the hunters burn out each spring and that are full again by autumn. From the fortress's wall the hunters watch the sun come up over the eastern sea before every hunt. Its town is Asahi Gate; its other places: Hinode Fortress, The Long Night Wall, Burned Village of Kitamura, Snow Monkey Springs, Orphans' Lodge, Frozen Pass of the Long Night, Hunters' Graveyard, Snowbound Trading Post, Breath Masters' Retreat, Yuki-onna's Valley, Watchfire Hill, Hunters' Supply Road. By land it joins Ayakashi Wood.

lore.name: District: Hyoga Reach
lore.info: Hyoga Reach is a district of the Asagiri Isles. An ice isle far north across White Strait: glaciers, black stone, a town of exiles, and the Sealing Vaults, a prison fortress built into the ice where the bodies of the great beasts lie bound, their power sealed into living hosts. The realm sends here what it cannot kill and dares not keep. The Hyoga Reach is the last place in the isles, and some of its exiles chose it. Its town is Shirokawa; its other places: The Sealing Vaults, Exiles' Shore Towns, Court of the Long Night, Glacier Road, Frozen Battlefield, Whaling Station, Ice Shrine of the White Stag, Black Stone Coast, Deserter Officers' Hut, Crevasse Field, Wardens' Watch Fort, Daylight Watch Ridge, Exiles' Graveyard. By land it joins nothing; by sea Kurosugi Range (across White Strait).

lore.name: District: Kurosugi Range
lore.info: Kurosugi Range is a district of the Asagiri Isles. A spine of black cedar mountains north of the capital, mist in every valley, paths that lead nowhere unless you know the sign. Two hidden villages sell their shinobi to whoever pays: Kagegi on the western slopes and Hayate on the eastern. They have been at peace for eleven years and at war for three hundred. The post road reaches only the outer checkpoint, and from a cove on the northern coast the only ferry to the ice isle crosses White Strait. Its town is Kagegi Village; its other places: Hayate Ridge Village, Mountain Temple of the Seven Falls, Valley of the Rank Exams, Hanging Bridge Pass, Ascetics' Peak, Woodcutters' Hamlet, Bear Den Ridge, Village Border Stones, Earth Spider Pits, Wind Shrine of the Pass, Snowline Huts, Monks' Herb Fields, Kagegi Outer Watchpost. By land it joins Ayakashi Wood, Miyako Plain, Veilgate; by sea Hyoga Reach (across White Strait).

lore.name: District: Mistmarsh Coast
lore.info: Mistmarsh Coast is a district of the Asagiri Isles. The eastern lowlands where the rivers lose themselves in reed and fog: stilt towns, smugglers' channels, drowned shrines in the shallows. The Kirisame clan of rain and poison keeps its compounds somewhere in the marsh and its debts in every town. Things that the capital wants lost are brought here to be lost. Its town is Ashiura; its other places: Mizuchi Naval Anchorage, Kirisame Stilt Village, The Drowned Lantern, Reed Channels, Drowned Village, Ashiura Fish Docks, Salt Marsh Shrine, Lighthouse of the Dragon's Eye, Sea Monk's Shallows, Smugglers' Rice Paddies, Old Coast Fort, Heron Island. By land it joins Fifty Stations Road, Seimei Bureau.

lore.name: District: Miyako Plain
lore.info: Miyako Plain is a district of the Asagiri Isles. The heartland: a broad river delta of rice paddies around Miyako, the walled castle city where the puppet emperor sits in his palace and the regent rules from the castle keep beside it. Samurai houses keep their mansions inside the walls and their quarrels in the streets; duels are fought at dawn on the river bridges. South of the walls the post road crosses at Oiwake, where the road down to the Ember Strait ferry begins. Its town is Miyako; its other places: Miyako Castle, The Inner Palace, Hidetsugu's Manor, Tournament Grounds, Hiwada Horse Fields, Straw Mask Hill Camp, Shogunate Rice Granary, Crossroads Gallows, Old Battlefield of Sekigane, Kappa River Fords, Ruined Summer Palace, Sun-Rite Shrine of the Plain, Hundred Fields Village. By land it joins Fifty Stations Road, Kurosugi Range, Seimei Bureau.

lore.name: District: Saikai Free Port
lore.info: Saikai Free Port is a district of the Asagiri Isles. The western harbour where the isles meet the open sea: a deep natural bay crowded with junks and the square-sailed ships of foreign traders, a town of lantern streets, gambling halls and warehouses that answer to the merchant guild rather than the regent. Ronin sell their swords here, shinobi buy passage under false names, and anything sold anywhere in the isles passes its quays first. The post road begins at its east gate and runs along the edge of the Blight toward the capital. Its town is Saikai; its other places: Guild Counting House, Foreign Quay Warehouses, Ronin Hiring Hall, Lantern Row Gambling Den, Saikai Lighthouse, Drifting Fish Market, Temple of Safe Voyages, Smugglers' Caves, Pirate Graves Reef, Foreigners' Quarter, Saltpan Village, Bayside Bathhouse. By land it joins Ashfall Blight, Fifty Stations Road.

lore.name: District: Seimei Bureau
lore.info: Seimei Bureau is a district of the Asagiri Isles. A lake city laid out on a precise grid inside a star-shaped ward wall, seat of the onmyoji college that reads the stars, names the lucky days, binds paper familiars and keeps the realm's wards. Nothing unwarded passes its gates by night. The Bureau and the shrines quarrel over who may exorcise what; both quarrel with the regent over who pays for it. Its town is Seimei; its other places: Bureau of Yin and Yang, Mask-Maker's Workshop, Lake of Stars, Paper Familiar Workshop, The Old Observatory, Talisman Market, Expelled Scholars' Quarter, Haunted Teahouse Lane, Lakeside Pleasure Boats, Moonview Bridge, Old Ward Stones, Bureau Dormitories. By land it joins Ayakashi Wood, Mistmarsh Coast, Miyako Plain.

lore.name: District: Tetsuyama
lore.info: Tetsuyama is a district of the Asagiri Isles. A volcanic isle south across Ember Strait: a smoking mountain whose slopes glow at night with forge towns. The isles' swordsmiths work here, and the masters among them fold Soul into steel and wake the spirits that sleep in the best blades. A blade awakened on Tetsuyama is named and remembered, and so is whoever carried it there. Its town is Hibana; its other places: Kurogane Iron Castle, Forge Guild Hall, The Deep Forges, Miners' Town, Lava Tubes, Crater Rim Shrine, Polishers' Street, Ember Vent Fields, Kurogane Armoury, Revenant Shaft, Hot Spring Inn, Black Sand Beach. By land it joins nothing; by sea Fifty Stations Road (across Ember Strait).

lore.name: District: Veilgate
lore.info: Veilgate is a district of the Asagiri Isles. A shrine city on the northwest cliffs above the Sea of Fog, built around a giant pale torii at the cliff's edge: the gate through which the Veil Court ferries the dead. Pilgrims come to say farewells, Veil Officers keep their living-side post here, and at night lanterns drift out over the fog. When the war dead pile up faster than they can be ferried, masked and hungry spirits climb back up the cliffs. Its town is Tasogare; its other places: Black Ferry Fortress, Grey Thread Shrine, The Great Gate Cliffs, Pilgrims' Hostel, Mask Shore, Hanging Lantern Village, Deserters' Gorge, Ferrymen's Rest, Weeping Torii, Old Battle Barrow, Fog Watch Tower, Moorland Graves. By land it joins Kurosugi Range.

lore.name: Empty Lanterns on the Night Road
lore.info: Empty lanterns are paper lanterns that float along the roads at night with nobody carrying them, lit with a light that gives no light. A traveller who looks closely sees that the glow casts no shadow and shows nothing of the ground. Those who follow one forget where they were going, and are found at dawn sitting by the roadside, unable to say why they left the inn. They are met on the Fifty Stations Road, in the streets around Seimei and on the cliff paths of Veilgate. Ghost Pine Hill is notorious for them, and station masters there warn travellers to be indoors by dark. Prayers and void-craft barely touch the light, though a blade can still tear the paper. Porters say the cure is to speak your destination aloud every few steps and to carry a lantern of your own with a real flame, so you can see which light throws a shadow. Dawn puts every empty lantern out.

lore.name: Entertainers and Storytellers
lore.info: Entertainers in the isles live on the road and on whatever a crowd will pay. Travelling theatre troupes carry carts of costumes and masks from town to town and play heroes, ghosts and famous swordsmen in inn yards and shrine grounds; Troupe-Master Sanshiro's company crossed to Hibana with a play about a smith who forged his own soul. Storytellers sit in inn baths and tea houses with a folding fan and tell ghost tales for a cup, as Tsurube the Storyteller does at the Seventh Station Inn. Biwa monks sing the old war verses, wandering flute players beg on bridges, poets sell a verse for a coin on the pleasure boats of Seimei, and drummers, jugglers and acrobats work every festival crowd. Musicians play koto and shamisen in the tea houses of the pleasure districts. Entertainers stand low in the law and need travel papers like anyone else at the barriers, but a famous one is fed and lodged free in every town that wants to hear him.

lore.name: Everyday Meals
lore.info: Everyday meals in the isles are built on rice. A family eats rice or rice gruel morning and evening, with soup, pickles and whatever its district adds, and anything left over becomes the next day's gruel. On the road a traveller carries three salted rice balls wrapped in bamboo leaf with a pickled plum in each, and longer journeys call for dried fish, roasted rice and miso balls packed in oiled paper. Townspeople buy much of their food ready-made from stalls: toasted rice cakes, noodles, grilled fish and soup ladled out at the post houses. Meat is rare except in the north and among hunters; fish, tofu and beans do its work everywhere else. Tea goes with every meal and sake with any meal that deserves it. Meals are eaten kneeling at low trays, the eldest or the highest-ranked served first. A guest is fed before any business is spoken of, and leaving rice in the bowl is rude, because someone grew it and someone was taxed on it.

lore.name: Execution at Crossroads
lore.info: When a crime earns death by Shogunate law, the execution happens at the nearest major crossroads so that all travellers might see it and know the law is enforced. The condemned is hanged from a wooden frame or executed by sword depending on their rank; a samurai is given a beheading rather than the rope. The body is left hanging for a day or two as warning, then cut down and given to family or the earth. A person hanged at a crossroads is said to haunt that place; some crossroads have shrines built by them for the dead to rest easier.

lore.name: Festivals of the Isles
lore.info: Festivals of the Isles mark the year district by district. Hinode Hold greets the First Sunrise of the year from the Asahi Gate with sun-steel raised. Tetsuyama holds the Mountain Fire Festival, carrying burning brands up to the Crater Rim Shrine while the forges of Hibana burn all night. The Mistmarsh Coast races its dragon boats through the reed channels, navy, smugglers and the rain clan all betting. Saikai blesses its trading fleet on the Night of the Hundred Ships, every ship lit with lanterns and the Temple of Safe Voyages' bell ringing. In the Ayakashi Wood the foxes hold their wedding procession on the Foxfire Night, and a human who sees it may be invited, warned off or tricked. In Miyako the Capital Tournament opens before the regent and every great house, and draws the best swords in the isles.

lore.name: Fishing on the Coasts
lore.info: Fishing feeds every coast of the isles and keeps most fishing families in debt. Boats go out before dawn with nets and lines, and the catch comes back to two very different markets. Off the shore near Saikai the boats lash themselves together into the Drifting Fish Market, where the catch is auctioned from deck to deck by lantern light and gone by sunrise, while women split and clean fish at speed on the gutting pier. At Ashiura on the Mistmarsh Coast every basket passes a tally-man who counts it and marks his board, and moneylenders walk the docks at the end of each day to collect. Fishing families buy their boats, nets and salt on credit and pay it back from the catch, so one bad season can sink a family for years. Mizuchi warships keep pirates off the fishing grounds and charge harbour dues for it, and the coast resents the dues more than it thanks them for the pirates. Sailors and marsh folk sew a blue-inked water ward into a sleeve against drowning.

lore.name: Food by District
lore.info: Food by district varies more than the isles' rice would suggest. Miyako Plain eats the rice it grows and sends its best to the capital, where the markets under the castle sell delicacies from every coast. The Mistmarsh Coast eats fish, eel and marsh herbs from its boardwalk stalls, and a careful visitor asks where the herbs came from. Saikai eats from every ship in the harbour, and the Foreigners' Quarter cooks in foreign ways that the rest of the port has started to borrow. On Tetsuyama the Kurogane feed their miners well, because hungry men do not dig. The hunters of Hinode Hold eat in a mess hall from the rice the supply carts haul up from the south. The exiles of the Hyoga Reach live on fish, seal and whatever the whale boats bring home. In the Ashfall Blight curse-bearers cook with the grey salt boiled from its springs. Seimei's lake gives the city its fish. In the Ayakashi Wood the tanuki night market roasts chestnuts and sells food that nobody should trust by morning.

lore.name: Forbidden Scrolls and Lost Arts
lore.info: There are techniques so dangerous or so strong that they are written into scrolls and hidden in temples, kept by only a few teachers and their chosen students. Some forbidden scrolls contain techniques that demand such sacrifice to learn that most people would die before mastering them. Others contain knowledge so corrupting that a person who learns it cannot be trusted in company. The Stolen Scroll, which started the cold war between Kagegi and Hayate villages, contained techniques that neither village will speak of openly; what matters is that someone died in its stealing. Not all forbidden knowledge is dark—some techniques are simply too powerful for the world to handle if they were common.

lore.name: Forms of Address
lore.info: A samurai is addressed by family name and honorific: a lord of House Takamori is Takamori-sama. Office goes before the name or replaces it: Admiral Mizuchi Naotora is 'the Admiral' on his own deck. A guild master is called master; a teacher called sensei; an elder called dono. To call a samurai by their personal name alone is an insult unless they give you permission. The common folk use family name or occupation: a carpenter is 'carpenter,' a fisherman 'fisherman,' an elder 'grandfather' or 'grandmother' with respect. Strangers use 'sir' or 'lady' with formality; friends use names more freely.

lore.name: Forms of Oath
lore.info: An oath is sworn by speaking the words clearly before witnesses and, often, before a shrine or faction officer. A binding oath may involve cutting the hand and mixing blood, signing a scroll with one's blood, or speaking the words three times to ensure they are truly meant. A broken oath marks a person as faithless: a faction betrayed by one of its sworn brands them a Turncoat and remembers it. An oath sworn to a faction is recorded by that faction's officers and tracked formally; an oath sworn between individuals is witnessed but less official, though no less binding in the eyes of the isles.

lore.name: Fox Spirits and the Fox Court
lore.info: Fox spirits are yokai of cunning and shape, dwelling throughout Ayakashi Wood and the lower lands in human shapes most of the time. Some foxes are young and impulsive, taking human lovers and causing chaos; others are ancient and wise, keeping to the shrines built for them. The Fox Court in the Wood's deepest groves is ruled by foxes of such age that few now remember them as anything but names and stories. Fox spirits are bound by their own honor: a fox who speaks a promise cannot break it, which makes their words careful and sparse. A human loved by a fox spirit is marked by it, and all other creatures know this and are wary. The greatest foxes can wear any human shape so perfectly that no one doubts, and they keep to themselves why they do it.

lore.name: Funayurei, the Ladle Ghosts
lore.info: Funayurei are the ghosts of drowned sailors, and every crew from the Mistmarsh Coast to the Saikai Free Port fears them in fog. They come up around a ship in pale crowds, hands reaching over the gunwale, asking for a ladle. A crew that gives a sound one is lost, for the dead bail the sea into the boat until it goes down. Careful sailors carry a ladle with its bottom knocked out and pass that over instead, and the ghosts scoop at nothing until the fog lifts. Swords and spears barely bite them. Prayers spoken with real feeling and the soul-blades of the Veil Court reach them where steel does not, and sunrise sends them back below. At Veilgate, where the dead are close, pilgrims on the cliff paths have seen them climbing out of the Sea of Fog, and fishermen there leave a bottomless ladle hanging by the door of every boat shed.

lore.name: Gambling and Debt
lore.info: Gambling in the isles runs on dice, cards and other people's money. The common game is two dice shaken in a cup and called odd or even, played on a mat in a gambling hall, a barracks or a smugglers' tavern; cards come next, and anything that can be bet on is bet on, from the dragon boats of the Mistmarsh to a quarrel in an inn yard. Saikai's Lantern Row has the loudest dens, and the loudest of them keeps a debt book on a lacquer stand where Smiling Okon writes down every coin she lends with a cheerful word. Honest bone dice are for sale, and the dens remember the faces of players who bring their own. Gambling debts are collected like any other, by moneylenders and by ronin hired from the halls, and a gambler who cannot pay may lose his sword, his house or his good name. The great houses frown on retainers who gamble, and an heir seen too often at the tables becomes the talk of the capital.

lore.name: Gashadokuro, the Starving Skeleton
lore.info: A gashadokuro is a giant skeleton built from the bones of the unburied dead, tall enough to look into a second-floor window. Folk on the Miyako Plain and in the Ashfall Blight say it gathers where battlefields and famine graves were left to the crows, and the people of Haibara say one is meant to rise from Bone Gully, where the old capital's dead were thrown. It walks only at night. The warning is a rattle like dry bamboo in the wind, and anyone who hears it is told to get indoors, because it bites off heads. A sword passes between its ribs; an arrow does the same. The old soldiers' advice is a hammer, a maul or a heavy staff to crack the bones, and to hold out for the dawn, which it cannot stand. Priests at Veilgate say the surest cure is the oldest: proper burial for the dead, so that there are no unburied bones for the next one to be made of.

lore.name: Giant Hornets of the Wood
lore.info: Giant hornets of the Ayakashi Wood and the Kurosugi Range are as long as a thumb, and one sting can kill a horse. They build paper nests in hollow trees and under banks of earth, and a nest defends itself in a cloud. Foragers and woodcutters learn to listen for the clicking of jaws, which is the hornets' warning, and to walk away slowly the moment they hear it. Running draws the cloud; swatting brings the whole nest. Late summer is the worst season, when the nests are largest and the hornets go hunting other insects. Villagers who must clear a nest do it at night with smoke and a sealed jar. The Mushiro insect-hosts of Kagegi Village keep tamer cousins that answer to them, but the wild hornets answer to nobody, and a Mushiro who walks into a wild nest is stung like anyone else.

lore.name: Grades of the Seimei Bureau
lore.info: The Seimei Bureau grades its people by examination. A Bureau Student wears white, sleeps in the long dormitories under the curfew bell and spends years on folding, ink, stars and the calendar. Passing the licence examinations set by the Talisman Master makes a student a Licensed Onmyoji, entitled to work anywhere in the isles and to sell talismans with a Bureau tablet on show; the licensed wear layered robes and a tall lacquered hat. Bureau Examiners test the students and inspect the market stalls that claim a licence. Bureau Masters teach, keep the great wards and read the stars for the houses. The Director's Hand is the small circle that carries out the Director's orders. Students take a blue brocade Learning Omamori into the examination hall for luck, and those who fail too often tend to end up reading palms in the Expelled Scholars' Quarter. Writing charms for sale without a licence is against the Bureau's rules, which is why the back-lane stalls are cheaper.

lore.name: Grades of the Shogunate's Officials
lore.info: The Shogunate's officials climb five grades, all of them in grey. A Clerk of the Grey copies registers, stamps travel papers and counts tax rice, and most officials begin and end their lives at that desk. A Warrant Officer carries a sealed warrant and the authority to search, arrest and escort; the constables under him carry the jitte, an iron truncheon with a side hook for catching a blade, so that prisoners come in alive. A Magistrate holds a district under warrant and hears its cases. A Councillor sits on the councils in Miyako Castle that write the law and set the rice tax. The Regent's Voice are the few who speak for the regent himself, and their letters are read as his. Villagers judge the grades by the escort: a clerk walks, a warrant officer rides with a constable or two, and a magistrate arrives with spears. A clerk's goodwill is cheap and worth having, since it is the clerk who decides which papers go to the top of the pile.

lore.name: Guild Houses
lore.info: Guilds keep their own order in the trades: the Tetsuyama Forge Guild, the Saikai Merchant Guild, and smaller guilds of carpenters, masons, weavers and smiths in every town. A guildmaster teaches apprentices and journeymen, sets prices in concert with other masters, and polices quality and theft. A guild apprenticeship lasts several years; a journeyman pays fees to work; a master owns their own shop and answers to the guild's council. A merchant who undercuts the guild's prices or a smith who sells shoddy work will find themselves cast out and unable to buy supplies or hire labour.

lore.name: Haibara, the Ash Town
lore.info: Haibara is the one town of the Ashfall Blight, and the isles know it as the last stop before the grey. It was raised from the timbers of the old war's fortresses, and the faded banners of both armies still hang in the yard of the Grey Banner Waystation. Its trades are grim ones: beds and clean water for travellers, cloth masks against the ash, guides for the Grey Pilgrims' Road, curse-breaking for a fee, and relics sold by candlelight at the Haibara Ash Market. Haibara people are thought hard and incurious; they have watched every kind of curse-bearer walk through and judge nobody by a mark. The Vow Temple brings the town its other traffic, as penitents and oath-takers come from every district to swear there. The Grey Pilgrimage sets out from Haibara to pray at the Fallen Gate of the old capital. A visitor should wear a cloth over mouth and nose, should never lean on or draw from the roped and sealed town well, and should never ask a curse-bearer what they carry. Nobody in Haibara swears at the Vow Temple in jest, and nobody buys at the night market without first asking how the thing hungers.

lore.name: Hair and Headwear
lore.info: Hair in the isles is a sign of station as plain as a crest. Samurai and most grown men of the towns wear a topknot, oiled and tied, glossy black on a young lord and grey on an old one, and a messy or wild topknot marks a gambler or a ronin who has stopped caring who notices. Monks of the Mountain Temple Order shave their heads, and an outlaw who takes the vow shaves with them. Women wear their hair long and pinned up with combs and pins; at court a lacquered hairpin with a coral bead can open doors before its wearer has said a word. Hair worn loose in public belongs to mourners, poets, the grief-stricken and the disreputable. Exiles in the north crop theirs short. Headwear finishes the picture: a deep straw hat for the road, a tall lacquered hat for a licensed onmyoji, a white headband brushed with a single word for a fighter going into a fight that matters, and a woven basket over the whole head for the wandering monks who play the flute for coins.

lore.name: Hayate Village
lore.info: Hayate Village is the younger shinobi village of the Kurosugi Range, built on the windy ridges above the passes where the Kazakiri cut the wind into blades, the Kusurigi keep their field-medicine herbs and the Okamura raise their fighting wolves. Hayate shinobi are fast, loud by Kagegi standards and proud of it, and they take the contracts Kagegi thinks beneath it: escorts, rescues, hunts. The passes owe Hayate their safety. Kagegi calls them upstarts; Hayate calls Kagegi a village that has forgotten how to laugh.

lore.name: Hibana, the Forge Town
lore.info: Hibana is the largest forge town on Tetsuyama's slopes, and every warrior in the isles who wants a great blade dreams of the day they climb from the Ember Pier to Forge Row. The town lives by steel: smiths and apprentices, charcoal burners, polishers, scabbard-makers, sulphur gatherers, ore carters, and the inns where buyers wait weeks for a commission. A guild-stamped katana costs about thirty Mon and a master's about ninety, and the ferry from Oiwake costs about thirty more. Hibana people are thought gruff, proud and impossible to hurry, and the saying elsewhere is that a Hibana smith will refuse a lord and serve a farmer if the farmer holds a sword better. Masters choose their customers, and a buyer waits on the bench outside a forge door until called in or sent away. The town's great night is the Mountain Fire Festival, when brands are carried up to the Crater Rim Shrine and the forges burn till dawn. A visitor must never touch a blade on a smith's rack, never walk into a forge uninvited, never haggle over a master's price, and never try to take a blade off the isle without a guild mark on it.

lore.name: Honour and Duels
lore.info: Honour is a sword's edge in the isles: a samurai's worth is measured by their name, their word and the way they face death. An insult to a samurai's honour must be answered with a blade, and a duel fought at dawn on neutral ground with witnesses is lawful killing. A duel is between two people alone; bringing allies or drawing a blade against an unarmed opponent is murder. A samurai who refuses a duel loses their house's name and becomes ronin; a commoner insulted by a samurai has no legal right to duel, though some do anyway and are either praised for courage or hanged for assault on a noble.

lore.name: Horse Breeding on the Plain
lore.info: Horse breeding in the isles belongs above all to House Hiwada, whose pastures on Miyako Plain run to the horizon and whose horses are the best in the isles and sold dear. Hiwada people ride from childhood and begin their service as grooms in the long stables, where every horse is known by name and the steward walks the aisles with an account book. Colts run in herds on open grass, are broken patiently and are taught to hold steady under a rider who shoots from the saddle at the gallop. The best become warhorses, heavy and brave, trained to kick and trample and to obey their own rider and no one else. Other horses go to the post stables of the Fifty Stations Road and to lords and rich merchants. Saddle, bridle and stirrups in Hiwada style are sold at the horse fields themselves. Most commoners never own a horse at all: on the plain carts are drawn by oxen, and on the mountain paths goods go by mule or on porters' backs.

lore.name: Hosts and the Birthright Beasts
lore.info: A host is a person who carries a sealed great beast's power inside them, bound into their body by a seal no living sealer fully understands. Hosts are born, chosen by desperate families, or made in war as weapons, and every faction that wants a beast's power wants the host who carries it. A host in harmony with the beast can draw on a fraction of its strength and survive the use; a host who loses their grip feels the beast's voice grow louder, its power bleed through, and in the end the seal can fail and the thing inside take over. Hosts learn to rest, to hold themselves steady and to keep their nature quiet, because a known host is a hunted one. To be a host is to be powerful and always at risk of becoming the cage itself.

lore.name: Hot Springs of the Isles
lore.info: Hot springs bubble up wherever the isles' fire runs close under the ground: on the slopes of Tetsuyama, along Bear Den Ridge in the Kurosugi Range, and at Snow Monkey Springs in the snows of Hinode Hold. The water smells of sulphur and minerals, and steam drifts across the slopes thickly enough that paths vanish into it and come out somewhere else. Folk believe the springs ease stiff joints, old wounds and the cough of the ash, and hunters stop to thaw their hands in them before going on. On Tetsuyama the smiths of Hibana use spring water for quenching, and swordsmen waiting on commissions soak at the Hot Spring Inn for weeks. Wild springs have their own manners: animals bathe in them too, the hottest pools can scald, and in winter the steam freezes into rime on the rocks around them. Nobody bathes in a spring that has gone quiet and stopped steaming.

lore.name: House Hiwada
lore.info: House Hiwada is the horse house of the plain: mounted archers who ride from childhood and shoot from the saddle at full gallop. Their sun-arrow crest guards the open country between the capital and the mountains, and Hiwada riders hunt bandits down the long roads that the post barriers do not reach. The house breeds the best horses in the isles and sells them dear. Farmers of the plain trust Hiwada riders more than any other samurai, because the Hiwada come when the bandits do; the capital thinks them rustic, loud and very hard to command.

lore.name: House Kurogane
lore.info: House Kurogane is the iron house: the great samurai family that holds Tetsuyama, its forges and its mines, and arms half the isles. Kurogane warriors fight in heavy lacquered iron that no ordinary blade can open, and they advance slowly and never step back. The house sends the regent its tribute in swords rather than rice, and every house's armoury carries the black iron crest, three interlocking rings in a circle, somewhere. The people of the volcanic isle call the Kurogane hard and fair: they work their miners to the bone and feed them well. In the capital they are called smiths with titles, and Kurogane lords have long memories for that.

lore.name: House Mizuchi
lore.info: House Mizuchi is the sea house, the great samurai family whose river-dragon crest flies from every warship in the isles. Its fleet holds the straits, escorts the rice barges to the capital and hangs pirates from the yardarm at Ashiura. Mizuchi samurai fight on rolling decks in light armour, with spear and grappling hook, and swim like seals. The coast loves them for keeping the sea lanes safe and hates them for the harbour dues. The other houses think them half fishermen; the Mizuchi think the other houses have never seen what comes out of the deep water at night.

lore.name: House Takamori
lore.info: House Takamori is the regent's own house, the oldest of the four great samurai houses of Miyako Plain, and its crane crest flies over the capital's inner gate. Takamori swordsmen are famous for the draw-cut: the blade leaves the scabbard and the fight is over. The house holds the regency in the dying emperor's name, keeps the post road's toll barriers, and judges disputes between the other houses. Its retainers are drilled in poetry as hard as in the sword, and they are expected to die well. To the common people of the plain the Takamori are order itself: taxes collected on time, bandits hanged at the crossroads, festivals paid for. To the other houses they are a family that has ruled in someone else's name for three generations and has forgotten it was ever borrowed.

lore.name: Houses and Homes
lore.info: Houses and homes in the isles are built of wood, paper and straw wherever there is no reason to build otherwise. A farmhouse on Miyako Plain is a thatched hall with an earth-floored kitchen at one end and raised wooden floors at the other, a sunken hearth at its centre and sleeping mats rolled away by day. Town houses are narrow, with a shop or workroom on the street and the family living behind it. Samurai mansions in Miyako stand behind walls and gates, with gardens, guard rooms and separate women's quarters. The districts change the pattern: marsh folk live on stilts over the reed channels and walk plank walks between their houses, Hayate lashes its roofs against the gale and hangs wind chimes from every eave, Tetsuyama's miners live in soot-black rows, and the exiles of the Hyoga Reach build in black stone against the cold. Shoes come off at the step in every house in the isles. Fire is the dread of every town street, and each ward keeps buckets, hooks and a watch bell.

lore.name: How Saikai Bought Its Freedom
lore.info: Saikai's freedom from the regent's tax is the port's proudest story, and the version told on the quays is simple: the merchants paid for it. When the regency was young and short of money, the tale goes, the merchant guild lent the Shogunate more than it could ever repay, and took its payment in a charter that left the port's customs house, quays and foreign trade in the guild's hands for good. The great houses tell it differently, as a bribe dressed up as a loan, and some samurai still call the port the regent's pawnshop. Either way, the guild's flag flies over the customs house and the regent's does not, and the guild has kept the town out of every quarrel between the houses since. Saikai folk say the arrangement has made everyone richer, including the regents who granted it, and they point out that every house in the isles borrows from the counting house sooner or later.

lore.name: How the Hidden Villages Began
lore.info: The founding of the hidden villages of the Kurosugi Range is told in the lowlands as a story of the old capital's wars. In that telling, families skilled in seals and secret work went up into the cedar mountains to sell their arts to every side without belonging to any, and built Kagegi in a mist valley no army could find. Hayate came later, the tale goes, founded on the windy ridges above the passes by shinobi who wanted contracts of their own, and the two villages have quarrelled ever since: border stones recut, contracts poached, and insults remembered for a hundred years at a time. Lowland folk say the villages were at war for three hundred years and have been at peace for eleven. The peace is thin. A forbidden scroll was stolen not long ago, someone died in the stealing, and neither village will say what the scroll held. What the villages teach their own children about their founding is not told to outsiders, and it is bad manners to ask.

lore.name: How the Kurogane Came to Tetsuyama
lore.info: House Kurogane has held Tetsuyama for so long that people forget the Tetsuyama Forge Guild was there first. The smiths of the volcanic isle worked the mountain's iron long before any samurai house ruled it, and the guild still keeps the oldest forge on the isle in its hall. The Kurogane came, the tale goes, in the years of the old capital's wars, when every house needed swords and the isle that made them had no army to protect it; they offered the smiths protection and stayed to rule. The bargain still shapes the isle. The Kurogane own the mines, the castle and the miners' wages, while the guild keeps its secrets, inspects every blade and decides who may call themselves a master. Hibana people sum it up in a proverb about the house holding the isle and the guild holding the fire, and each side repeats it with a different emphasis. Every regent since has taken Kurogane tribute in swords, and the capital has never quite forgiven the house for being indispensable.

lore.name: How the Regency Came to House Takamori
lore.info: The regency began, as the plain tells it, with a child on the throne. An emperor died leaving an heir too young to rule, and the court, afraid of the great houses, gave the regency by imperial brush to the head of House Takamori, the oldest of the four great houses of Miyako Plain, to govern until the boy came of age. The regents of those years built the Shogunate's machinery: magistrates with warrants, grey-coated tax offices, and councils that sit in the castle rather than the palace. The heir grew up, yet the regency never ended, and it has passed from one Takamori lord to the next for three generations. How it outlived its reason depends on who is telling it. Takamori retainers say the emperors found the weight of rule too heavy and were glad to set it down; the court says the brush was lent and never given back. The present regent has governed for twenty years, and it was his doubling of the rice tax that raised the Straw Masks.

lore.name: Hunter Ranks on the Long Night Wall
lore.info: Hunter ranks on the Long Night Wall are earned in the snow. A Hunter Recruit is often an orphan raised at the Orphans' Lodge, drilling with wooden swords until the First Sunrise, when the orphans who lasted the winter are handed their first real blades. A Sworn Hunter has taken the oath, wears the Hold's dark uniform under a patterned haori and takes turns on the wall. A Hunter Captain leads a watch on the wall or a patrol beyond the gate. A Breath Master has carried one breathing school's forms as far as they go, trains that school's hunters and wears a coat in its colours. The Commander's Hand are the hunters Commander Asahina Tetsu sends where she cannot go herself. Recruiters walk the supply road south to the villages looking for orphans and volunteers, and the quartermaster's carts bring rice and steel up the same road. Promotion follows the Demon Nights: a hunter who holds the wall through them is remembered when a captain's place falls empty.

lore.name: Infamy on the Road
lore.info: The isles forgive a great deal of killing, in duels, wars and hunts, and none of the needless kind. Kill the surrendered, the fleeing, the bystander or the one a road's story depended on, and the road hears of it: first the name is whispered, then the toll barriers have your description and every honest door closes, and at the last a price goes on your head in every province and the bounty hunters ride. The vow temple at Haibara takes penance, a little at a time and never twice in quick succession; the dead stay dead.

lore.name: Inns and Guest Customs
lore.info: An inn provides a bed, a meal and the shelter of walls for travellers. Guests remove their shoes in the common room and leave weapons by the door unless the innkeeper knows them well. The innkeeper's word rules: noisy guests are asked to leave, fights inside the inn are ejected by the nearest samurai or guard, and theft is a hanging matter if the innkeeper chooses to pursue it. A guest who pays and keeps the peace is welcomed back; a guest who causes trouble is remembered. The better inns keep separate rooms for nobles and keep their fires warm through the winter.

lore.name: Inugami, the Bound Dogs
lore.info: Inugami are dog spirits made by a cruel rite and bound to a family's grudge. The family names an enemy, and the dog spirit hunts that person, slipping into them to sicken them from the inside: fever, a hunger that cannot be filled, barking in the sleeper's throat. Folk in the Ashfall Blight and the Kurosugi Range whisper about families said to keep inugami, and such families find their daughters hard to marry. The Inugami Kennels near Haibara, where an old curse-family once made the spirits, are a ruin now, but Haibara folk say the family is gone and the dogs are not. Curses and arrows do little against an inugami. Fire and sunlight hurt it, and the curse-hunters teach that the surest weapon is its name: whoever learns the true name of a bound dog can turn it back on the house that bound it. Nobody in the Blight shares a meal with someone who keeps a dog's skull on the family shelf.

lore.name: Jorogumo and Tsuchigumo: The Spider Women
lore.info: Jorogumo are yokai of seduction and cunning, spiders that learned human shape and human desires. They build their lairs in high places—cliff caves, ruined towers, old temples—and hunt travelers who stray from the path. A jorogumo is often beautiful enough that people willingly climb toward her, and by the time they understand, the web has already caught them. Tsuchigumo are earth-spiders, more bestial and less clever, dwelling in burrows and caves, and they are far less dangerous to travelers than jorogumo. Both kinds can grow to enormous size if they hunt successfully for centuries. They do not have a spider-court and do not keep law, but the old jorogumo in distant places have their own aristocracy of old grudges and ancient pride. A person caught by a jorogumo's web might bargain their way free if they are clever, but few escape twice.

lore.name: Kagegi as Visitors Know It
lore.info: Kagegi Village is the older of the two hidden villages of the Kurosugi Range, and the post road treats it as a town like any other even though most of it is closed to strangers. The isles know it as a place of mountain guides, hunters and hired shinobi, where lords and merchants send their stewards to buy a contract at the Mission Hall. The valley's other trades are cedar, herbs and the escort of travellers down the guarded path to the cove where the White Strait ferry puts in. Kagegi people are thought quiet, courteous and unreadable, and farmers of the plain say a Kagegi man can stand beside someone for an hour before being noticed. Every visitor is met at the Outer Checkpoint, searched and escorted, and the custom is to submit with good grace. A guest must never leave the escort's path, never wander toward the training grounds or the clan compounds, never ask a shinobi's real name or clan, and never speak well of Hayate at a Kagegi table. A price named in the Mission Hall is not haggled over; clients who try are shown out politely and are not let in again.

lore.name: Kagegi Village
lore.info: Kagegi Village is the older of the two shinobi villages of the Kurosugi Range, hidden in a cedar valley where the sun reaches the floor for an hour a day. Its clans (Kurobane shadow-binders, Mushiro insect-hosts, Yumeno mind-walkers, Karakuri puppeteers) sell their skills to the houses as spies, guards and assassins under contract, and the village takes its cut. Kagegi shinobi are patient, quiet and thorough, and the village's word on a contract is worth more than a samurai's oath. The valley folk revere the village; the houses use it and fear it.

lore.name: Kamaitachi, the Sickle Weasels
lore.info: Kamaitachi are the sickle weasels, three of them riding a single whirlwind: the first knocks the traveller down, the second cuts, and the third salves the cut so that it does not bleed. The victim gets up, walks on and finds the long clean wound only later. Woodcutters in the Kurosugi Range, hunters of Hinode Hold and porters on the Fifty Stations Road all have the scars, and every one of them says the same thing: there was a gust, a stumble, and nothing more. Kamaitachi cut for fun and are gone before anyone can turn round. A blade only catches the wind they ride, and the wind is their own. Folk wisdom is to drop low behind a stone wall or a bank of earth when a sudden dust devil comes spinning down the path, and some porters carry a pouch of grit to throw into it. A heavy stick swung into the whirlwind has been known to bring one tumbling out, very angry and much smaller than its reputation.

lore.name: Kappa of River and Lake
lore.info: Kappa are yokai of water, small and armored, dwelling in rivers and lakes of the isles where they are mostly content to ignore the living. They are mischievous and oddly honorable: if a kappa swears an oath, the water itself enforces it. Most kappa hunt fish and small animals, but a hungry or lonely kappa might drag a person into the water for drowning, which is how they reproduce: kappa are born in such moments. The strongest kappa can pull down ships, and those few are feared by the Mistmarsh fishers and the port sailors. Kappa respect strength and courtesy in equal measure; a person who bows to a kappa and swears to leave an offering might cross its water unmolested.

lore.name: Kitsunebi Crossing's Customs
lore.info: Kitsunebi Crossing is the town at the edge of the Ayakashi Wood where the human road meets the yokai paths, and the isles know it as the one place where the two trade openly. It lives from the crossing itself: the Fox Shrine Post where coaches stop, guides for the wood's edge, bamboo shoots and mushrooms from the near groves, fried tofu for the shrine, and the Lantern Market of the Wood, where stallkeepers who are not quite human sell to people who are. Crossing folk are thought odd, mild and very careful with words; they do not say thank you for a gift until they know what it costs. The fox shrine is respected by humans and yokai alike, and the town keeps its peace under it. A visitor should leave fried tofu at the shrine, bow to anyone who bows first, and promise nothing lightly, since a promise made here may be collected. Nobody should pay at the night market with a name, a year or a memory, eat food offered on the Foxfire Night without asking who cooked it, or follow lights into the trees after dusk.

lore.name: Kodama and Tree-Spirits
lore.info: Kodama are spirits of the old cedars and camphor trees of Ayakashi Wood, small and bright-eyed, mostly harmless unless you cut down their tree. When a kodama's tree falls, the spirit either dies with it or goes mad with rage, and a maddened kodama will haunt a forest for decades, causing travelers to lose their way and trees to fall unexpectedly. The ancient kodama in the deepest groves—those in trees hundreds of years old—are wise and curious, and some of them trade knowledge with humans in exchange for protection of their woods. To earn a kodama's trust is to have a guide in Ayakashi Wood's twisting paths; to anger one is to have the forest itself as an enemy.

lore.name: Lacquerwork
lore.info: Lacquerwork in the isles starts with urushi, the raw sap of the lacquer tree, sold in pots on Polishers' Street and dreaded for the rash it raises on careless hands. It is brushed on in thin coats, each left to harden in a damp, dust-free room and then rubbed smooth before the next goes on, so a fine piece takes many coats and many weeks. Once you look, lacquer is everywhere: the black iron plates of Kurogane armour, sword scabbards, hairpins at court, the stand that holds a gambling den's debt book, the case of a physician's kit, the tall hats of licensed onmyoji, theatre masks and the bodies of fighting puppets. Black and red are the common colours, and gold dust sprinkled into wet lacquer marks work made for lords and the court. A lacquered piece outlasts its owner, so households hand down their lacquered trays, bowls and writing cases for generations. A lacquerer's apprentice spends the first years grinding, sieving and suffering the rash before being trusted with a brush.

lore.name: Legends of the Ruined Summer Palace
lore.info: The Ruined Summer Palace on Miyako Plain was an emperor's summer retreat until it was abandoned three reigns ago, and it is the plain's favourite ghost story. The tale told in the rice villages is that a reign ended badly there, and that its ill will stayed behind in the halls when the court packed up and left. Since then the roofs have fallen, the gardens have run wild around a stagnant pond, and black clouds gather over the palace on still nights while the sky elsewhere stays clear. Villagers point at those clouds and call them the old reign's curse brooding, and they will not plant or build within sight of the walls. No traveller camps in the ruins, birds do not nest in the eaves, and the frogs of the garden pond fall silent all at once for no reason anyone can see. Pedlars who cross the plain at night go the long way round. Mothers on the plain quiet their children with the threat of being left at the summer palace for a night.

lore.name: Letters and Couriers
lore.info: Letters and couriers hold the isles together. A letter is brushed on folded paper, wrapped and closed with the sender's seal: a merchant presses his carved signet, a lord his crest and an official the Shogunate's seal. The Post-Road Wardens carry the mail the length of the Fifty Stations Road, their riders in blue changing horses at each station and riding on through the night when a dispatch is urgent. Off the highway, letters travel with whoever is going that way, merchants, pilgrims, ferrymen and monks, paid with a coin or a favour. The great institutions keep their own couriers: the Seimei Bureau sends young onmyoji with sealed cases of talismans to the capital, and the hidden villages pass word by runners and by mirrors flashed from their watchtowers. Professional letter-writers sit near every market for those who cannot write, and some of them read the letters back to people who cannot read. A letter carried privately is only as safe as its carrier, and every house knows it.

lore.name: Magistrates and Warrants
lore.info: A magistrate holds a warrant from the Shogunate that gives them power to judge disputes, arrest the accused and pass sentence in their district. Magistrates are chosen for their incorruptibility or their connections, often both; a good magistrate is trusted more than a lord, and a corrupt one is hanged when he is caught. They keep offices in the main town of each district, hear cases in the morning and rule by afternoon, and their judgment stands unless appealed to the Shogunate's own courts in Miyako. A warrant issued by a magistrate can cross any district's border; the post road respects it and every lord does too, because resisting a magistrate is resisting the reign itself.

lore.name: Magma Crawlers of the Lava Tubes
lore.info: Magma crawlers are glowing lizards as big as an ox that live in the lava tubes under Tetsuyama's volcano. Their bellies shine through the cracks in their plated hides, and they lie in heaps on the warmest stone, moving slowly unless something comes into their tunnels. Then they defend their heat. A crawler's bite melts what it closes on, and fire, hammers and the stone of the mountain do it little harm. Hibana folk who go down into the Lava Tubes wrap wet cloths over mouth and nose and take water, because water is the one thing a crawler fears: a full bucket thrown over one makes it hiss, steam and stiffen into dark stone until it warms again. Sulphur gatherers say a crawler seen near the surface means the mountain is restless, and young smiths are told never to follow the warmth deeper into a tube than the light reaches.

lore.name: Markets and Trading
lore.info: Every town large enough to hold a market has one: a square or riverbank where merchants spread their goods on cloth and shout their prices, where common folk sell what they grew or made, and where news and rumour travel as freely as goods. Market days are usually once a ten-day; a merchant pays a small fee to the town magistrate for space and protection. Trading is loud, haggling is expected, and a handshake seals a deal unless the price is large enough to need witnesses. Merchants who cheat the measure or sell spoiled goods are pilloried or, in the worst cases, have a hand taken.

lore.name: Marriage and Households
lore.info: A marriage is arranged by families and sealed with gifts and a shrine ceremony; love is hoped for but not required. A wife joins her husband's household and takes his family name, though her own house's name remains in her courtesy title. Children belong to the father's house. A samurai's wife is expected to manage the household, keep counsel, and bear sons; a merchant's wife often works the business alongside her husband. Divorce is rare but permitted if the woman's father and husband agree; a woman who leaves her husband without permission loses all standing in her birth family.

lore.name: Marsh Vipers
lore.info: Marsh vipers are the grey snakes of the Mistmarsh reeds, also found in the ditches and dead orchards of the Ashfall Blight, and their bite brings a burning fever. A viper strikes when it is stepped near and flees otherwise, so marsh folk walk the reed paths tapping a staff ahead of them and never put a hand into a clump of reeds they cannot see into. Every household in the marsh keeps the antidote, a bitter brew in a small corked bottle, and travellers are advised to carry some before they leave Ashiura. The Kirisame Clan milks the vipers for their poison, and marsh folk say a rain-clan stranger who walks the reeds without a staff is carrying something better than antidote. A viper bite on the road is treated at once: the wound cut, the poison drawn and the victim kept still.

lore.name: Mask Lords and Great Masks
lore.info: Mask lords and great masks are the oldest and worst of the masked hungry dead, and the Veil Court names them before any other danger. A great mask is a towering spirit that has eaten hundreds of lesser ones; it walks through the fog of Veilgate on tide nights, mindless and ravenous, and has been seen on the ice of the Hyoga Reach. Swords, arrows and clubs do little against it. A mask lord is rarer and worse: a masked spirit that has got its mind and will back, human-sized again, articulate and cruel. It commands lesser masks, bargains with the living, and wants a body. Poison means nothing to either, and curses nothing to a mask lord. Only void and the soul-blades of the Veil Court truly wound them. Folk in Tasogare have one rule about them: a mask that howls can be outrun, but a mask that speaks sensibly and offers you something is the one to flee from. When the Fog Watch Tower's bell rings, the town bars its doors.

lore.name: Mask-Making
lore.info: Mask-making in the isles serves the theatre, the festivals and plain hard work. Theatre masks are carved from cedar and finished in many coats of lacquer so that a face seems to change as the actor tilts it; the finest are carved in a back-alley workshop in Seimei whose old mistress turns most customers away, and the lake city's actors queue at her door regardless. Festival masks are cheaper and brighter: white foxes with red markings, snarling red oni of lacquered wood and pale theatre faces, sold at any outfitter and worn by children and revellers whenever there is a festival crowd. Working masks are made of cloth. Shinobi wear a dark wrap that leaves only the eyes, breath hunters wear a half-mask of cloth and leather packed with herbs against smoke and demon breath, and the people of Haibara tie cloth over their mouths and buy fresh herb packets for them against the ash. Carvers say a mask is finished only when it looks different by lamplight than it did by day.

lore.name: Medicine and Healers
lore.info: Medicine in the isles is sold by apothecaries in every town, carried by travelling medicine-sellers and given away by monks. An apothecary's shelves hold charcoal antidote pills in paper packets, poultices of comfrey and rice paste for breaks and bruises, and physicians' kits of needles, silk thread, moxa and a small knife in a lacquered box. Travelling sellers such as Gensuke the Medicine-Seller walk the isles with a tall box of drawers on their backs, leave remedies at houses on credit and come back a year later to be paid for whatever was used. The monks of the Mountain Temple of the Seven Falls grow herbs on terraces and hand them to the poor, the Kusurigi clan of Hayate keeps field-medicine gardens on the ridges, and the hunters of Hinode carry packets of boiled linen and blood-stopping moss. Physicians grind kappa shell for setting bones, and marsh folk burn coils of chrysanthemum paste through the night against marsh fever. Bone-setters, midwives and needle doctors work in most towns for Mon or rice.

lore.name: Merchants and Trade
lore.info: A merchant buys goods cheap, sells them dear, and the difference is his profit. Saikai merchants are wealthy because they control the foreign trade and can buy tax-free; local merchants in small towns buy and sell what the region produces. A caravan merchant hires guards, buys goods in one town, sells them in another, and travels the post road most of his life. A merchant's word is his bond; if a merchant is caught cheating, his guildmaster can strip him of his standing and he cannot work anywhere in the isles. The best merchants are respected as much as samurai; a failed harvest or bad trade can bankrupt a house but enrich a quick-thinking merchant.

lore.name: Mining and Metalwork
lore.info: The volcanic isle of Tetsuyama holds iron and some copper; mines run deep into the mountain and are worked by labourers in terrible heat. A miner earns more than a farmer because the work is harder and shorter-lived; most miners do not work past thirty. The forges of Tetsuyama turn the ore into steel, and the master smiths forge the best blades in the isles. A sword takes weeks to forge, and the cost is high enough that most commoners never own one. The Tetsuyama Forge Guild guards its secrets—the technique of folding, the heat of the forges, the master-smiths' names—as closely as any shinobi village.

lore.name: Miyako, the Castle City
lore.info: Miyako is the capital of the isles, the walled city where the regent's white castle and the emperor's palace stand side by side, and the rest of the realm knows it for three things: government, swords and gossip. Its trades follow the court and the great houses: silk, lacquer and fine blades, rice brokers on the river docks, scribes, clerks and petition-writers, and the teachers of a great many sword schools. Capital people are thought proud, sharp-tongued and fond of rank, and country folk say a Miyako merchant bows lower than anyone and means it less. Every great house keeps a mansion inside the walls, and the street knows every crest; just now the white lotus and the crane are both worn openly. The city's great occasion is the Capital Tournament, fought on the Sand Ring before the regent and every house. A visitor must never brawl in the streets, since duels belong on the river bridges at dawn with witnesses, and should step aside and bow when a lord's procession passes. Anyone admitted to the Inner Palace leaves their sword at the Gate of Ceremonies. Talk of the emperor's health is common in teahouses and foolish within earshot of the castle's grey-coated officials.

lore.name: Mon and Price
lore.info: Mon is the currency of the isles: small bronze coins stamped with the emperor's seal. A typical labourer earns three to five Mon a day. Ordinary prices: a night at an inn in a town costs two or three Mon, a simple meal one Mon, a cup of sake a few copper fractions. Plain clothes cost about six Mon at an outfitter, a good mask four to six, lacquered armour twelve; a coach seat to the next district about twelve, a strait ferry about thirty. A guild-stamped katana costs about thirty Mon and one from a named smith about ninety, a month of a labourer's wages; a horse costs more than most villages own. The poor save Mon for a year to buy a blade; the rich measure their wealth in land and rice, not coin, though coin buys what coin can.

lore.name: Mountain Wolves
lore.info: Mountain wolves are the grey wolves of the high ranges, hunting in packs through the Kurosugi Range, Hinode Hold and the Ayakashi Wood. They follow travellers for a long time before they act, testing from the dark beyond the firelight, and they take the weak, the hurt and the alone. A party that keeps its fire high and stands together usually sees nothing but eyes. Hunters teach the same rule to every recruit: never run, never turn your back, raise a burning brand and hold your ground, and the pack backs away. Hayate Ridge Village keeps wolves in pens, and its wolf-handlers fight beside them, but a handler's partner obeys only its handler, and nobody else should try to feed one. Shepherds and woodcutters hang bells on their animals in winter, and a pack's howling on three nights running is taken as a reason to stay home.

lore.name: Names and Naming
lore.info: Children receive a name at birth from their parents, often inspired by a virtue, a place or an ancestor's name. When a child reaches adulthood, they may earn a second name through a deed or a title; some are famous enough that their earned name replaces their birth name in people's mouths. Nicknames attach themselves to people: a scarred samurai becomes 'the Scar,' a clever trader 'Fox-Tongue,' a brave fool 'Heart-Bringer.' A person's full name puts the family before the personal name, as in Lord Kurogane Tadakatsu; a commoner without a family name is known by trade or town, as in 'the cooper of Saikai'. Renaming oneself is the prerogative of the ronin and the outcast.

lore.name: News and Gossip
lore.info: News and gossip travel the isles faster than the post riders. Official news comes as notices pasted up at toll barriers, post stations and market squares: new laws, tax days, warrants and bounties under a magistrate's seal. Everything else goes by mouth. Tea benches on the road, like Granny Kiku's at the Rice-Cake Peddlers' Rest, hear every traveller's tale for the price of a cup; inn baths and bathhouses carry merchants' talk; porters swap stories about the people they carried; sledges bound for Asahi Gate trade gossip at the Snowbound Trading Post; and the Castle Market in Miyako sells gossip from every house beside its silk. Rumours grow as they travel, so a duel won on the post road can be a massacre by the time it reaches Saikai. Those who live by news, merchants, shinobi, magistrates and moneylenders among them, pay for it, and a servant who listens at the right screen can earn more from what she hears than from her wages.

lore.name: Nine-Tailed Fox and the Old Powers
lore.info: In the deepest groves of Ayakashi Wood, the Nine-Tailed Lady dwells, a fox so old that she remembers when the isles' borders were still being drawn. She has seen shinobi villages rise from nothing, watched the great houses war with each other, observed the sealed beasts being bound into their vaults. She rarely speaks to humans, and when she does, her words are cryptic and seem to change meaning the more a person thinks about them. The Nine-Tailed Lady's favor is worth more than gold, but earning it requires more than bargains: it requires time, patience, and understanding that you might spend years gaining what will never be enough. Some say she still remembers when foxes were gods and humans were small creatures in the grass. Others say that's exactly what she wants them to think.

lore.name: Nure-onna, the Wet Woman
lore.info: The nure-onna is the wet woman of the marsh channels: a great serpent with a woman's head and long wet hair, met on a riverbank or a mud bar in the Mistmarsh Coast holding out a bundle like a swaddled child. She asks the traveller to hold it for a moment. Whoever takes the bundle finds it growing heavy as a millstone and cannot let go, and she feeds while they are pinned. Marsh folk teach children never to take anything from a stranger on the water's edge, and boatmen keep a lit pot of coals in the bow when they pass the lonelier reed banks, because fire drives her off. She speaks little, and what she says is a lie told well. Swords slide on her scales and water is her home, but a thrown stone or a shovel of earth hurts her more than steel. Smugglers who work the channels by night know the difference between a woman calling for help and one who only holds out her arms.

lore.name: Oaths and Brotherhood
lore.info: An oath sworn before a faction officer binds a person to that faction's cause, sealed with words and the taking of a token. The sworn may rise through the faction's ranks by its jobs, its missions and the merit they earn, and the faction treats them by their standing. Holding oaths to two factions is allowed while they do not collide; a person caught working against one faction while sworn to another is branded a Turncoat by the betrayed side, and that brand follows them. Oaths between friends are witnessed rather than recorded, but they are kept as seriously. Needless killing, not broken faith, is what brands a person Notorious or Barred on the roads.

lore.name: Offices of a Samurai Household
lore.info: A samurai household is run by its offices as much as by its swords. The lord sits at its head. A steward keeps the accounts, the stores and the servants, and walks the storehouses and stables with an account book in hand. Hatamoto are the senior bannermen, who hold land or command in the lord's name and sit in his councils. Ordinary retainers stand the castle guard, ride escort and run the lord's errands, and most of them never rise further. Ashigaru are not samurai at all but farm boys with spears and borrowed armour, raised for a campaign and sent home for the harvest. Around every lord is a small circle of trusted swords who carry his word and act for him, and to be called the lord's hand is the highest trust a retainer can win. Retainers are paid a stipend in rice, so everyone in a household knows everyone else's worth to the last bale, and a quarrel over precedence at a feast can outlast a war.

lore.name: Offices of the Imperial Household
lore.info: The offices of the imperial household are old, few and jealously kept. Palace Servants clean, carry and keep the lesser doors. Gentlemen of the Court are the sons of the old noble families, who attend the ceremonies and write the court's poetry. Chamberlain's Agents do the business of the Grand Chamberlain, who keeps the seals, the calendar and the doors of the Inner Palace. Courtiers of the Inner Rooms serve close to the emperor's person, and the Keeper of the Regalia guards the sacred treasures in their cases. Priests of the sun rites keep the Sun-Rite Shrine of the Plain and bless the rice each spring, and ladies-in-waiting run the women's rooms. None of these offices carries a sword or commands a soldier. Their power is precedence and the brush: a courtier knows who may sit where, who may see whom and whose name is written first on a decree, and the Shogunate needs that knowledge as much as it pretends not to.

lore.name: Offices of the Veil Court
lore.info: The offices of the Veil Court run from Veil Cadet, a new officer still learning the court's law and the weight of a soul-blade, through Veil Officer, Veil Lieutenant and Veil Commander, up to The Marshal's Hand, who carry the Marshal's word between posts. Every officer also belongs to a division, and the living usually know them by that rather than by rank. Ferry officers guide the dead across; Healing officers mend the wounds spirits leave; Pursuit officers hunt deserters; Records and Research officers keep the lists of the dead and study them; the Gate Guard holds the cliffs. A commander keeps a post, as at the great pale torii in Tasogare, and captains lead a division's officers under her. All of them wear the black coat with the gate crest on the back. Officers may look young and be very old, and seniority goes by service, so a cadet who looks fifty can answer to a lieutenant who looks twenty.

lore.name: Oiwake, the Crossroads Station
lore.info: Oiwake Station is the crossroads of the isles, the one stop on the Fifty Stations Road that every traveller passes sooner or later.
