The town lives on the road: common inns and the Honjin Inn for lords, the post stable that changes coach horses, porters, grooms, rice-cake sellers, medicine peddlers, and the toll barrier that takes its fee from all of them. Oiwake folk are brisk, nosy and polite in the way of people who serve strangers for a living; it is said they forget a face in a day and a bad debt never. The town is famous for news, since four roads bring it in at once from the port, the capital, the marsh coast and the south strait. A seat on a coach to the next town costs about twelve Mon, and the ferry for Hibana leaves from the road south. A visitor must have papers ready at the barrier and must never draw steel in a station yard, which the Post-Road Wardens treat as a crime against the road itself; even the duelists of the Hundred-Duel Circuit take their quarrels elsewhere. When a lord is lodging at the Honjin Inn, commoners give way in the street and keep their voices down.

lore.name: Old Age and the Elderly
lore.info: Old age in the isles is honoured in speech and not always in practice, and the elderly know the difference. A family's elders get the warmest place by the hearth and the first bowl, and their word settles family quarrels. When the head of a household grows too old to work, he hands the house and its business to an heir and retires to advise, garden, write verse or take temple vows. Many never retire at all: old smiths sit outside the forges of Hibana every day watching the young ones work, and old women sell rice cakes on the post road into their eighties. Temples take in the old who have no family left, and the Mountain Temple of the Seven Falls keeps guest cells where they can rest. The poor fear old age most, since a widow without sons may end up stopping samurai in the street with a petition. Long life is counted a blessing from the kami, and a family marks an elder's sixtieth year with a feast and a red garment, as if the old person were beginning life again.

lore.name: Onmyoji Wards and Protective Seals
lore.info: Onmyoji ward their homes and places of work with signs written on paper and silk, sealing the soul-current into patterns that turn aside spirits, curses, and demons. A simple ward might protect against hunger spirits; a more complex one might lock a place against all yokai or bind demons inside a circle. The wards must be renewed as they fade, and a ward broken leaves a gap that hungry things can see. The most powerful wards are drawn by master onmyoji over weeks, incorporating the location's own earth and sky into the seal. Some wards are so old that no one remembers when they were written, but they still hold: the ward at the edge of Ashfall Blight has kept the curse-fog from spreading since the war that made the Blight. A person who knows the signs can learn to draw a simple ward to protect a room; learning the complex wards takes study at the Seimei Bureau and thirty years of careful work.

lore.name: Outcasts and the Barred
lore.info: An outcast is made by station: a servant without a master, a child of unmarried parents, a foreigner without a house. The Barred are made by deeds. A person who kills needlessly (the surrendered, the fleeing, the bystander) grows Notorious along the roads, and past that point they are Barred: lawful halls, coach yards and most inns refuse them, and barrier guards turn them back or hold them for judgment. Kill needlessly enough and the whole isles want them dead on sight, with bounty hunters on their trail. Penance done at a temple or shrine, honestly and over time, can wear the mark down; the memory of it lingers in the towns longer than the mark itself.

lore.name: Paper and Ink
lore.info: Paper and ink are the raw materials of half the isles' crafts. Paper is made from mulberry bark, beaten, soaked to pulp and lifted from water on screens in thin sheets, then sized with rice starch so that ink will not run. Bamboo goes into coarser sheets and into brush handles, lantern frames and umbrella ribs. Black ink is pine soot bound with glue and pressed into sticks, ground on an inkstone with a little water before writing, and red cinnabar ink is the colour wards and seals are written in. Seimei is the centre of the trade: its Talisman Market sells blank ward paper, ink cakes and brush sets beside the finished charms, and the Bureau's students go through stacks of white sheets folding paper familiars. Ordinary paper ends up as letters, ledgers, sliding screens, prayer strips, folding lanterns and the wishes hung on bamboo at the Star Festival. A household that owns good paper and an inkstone is, in the eyes of its neighbours, a household that can read.

lore.name: Post Stations
lore.info: A post station is a wayhouse on the Fifty Stations Road where a traveller can stable a horse, sleep, eat and change mounts if they are riding the post. Each station has a station master, grooms, cooks and servants, all employed by the Post-Road Wardens. A simple night's sleep costs two or three Mon; a meal costs one. A fresh horse from the post stables costs five Mon a day. The stations are uniform by design: a central hall with a hearth, a sleeping room for commoners, a separate room for nobles or the wealthy, stables and a kitchen. The mail rider changes horses at each station and rides on; merchants sometimes spend days waiting for the roads ahead to clear.

lore.name: Prayers at the Weeping Torii
lore.info: The Weeping Torii is a lone gate on the Veilgate moor that is always wet with dew, and the pilgrims of Tasogare believe grief is heard there. The tale says the gate began to weep the year a mother knelt beneath it for a child lost at sea and would not get up, and that it has never dried since. Mourners walk out from the Pilgrims' Hostel each morning to kneel in the wet grass with a written name or some small belonging of the one they have lost, and walk back before dark. Some tie folded paper to the posts, and when the damp washes out the ink within the day, the pilgrims take it as a sign that the message has been read. It is thought bad luck to wipe the posts dry or to shelter under the crossbeam from the rain. Nobody goes there at night, and a pilgrim who finds the gate dry is advised to go home and come back another day.

lore.name: Puppet-Making
lore.info: Puppet-making in the isles is both a stage craft and a war craft. Stage puppets are carved and lacquered with jointed limbs and worked by puppeteers dressed in black, sometimes three to a single puppet, in plays of heroes, foxes and ghosts at festivals and in town theatres. The fighting puppets of the Karakuri clan of Kagegi Village are the same craft taken further: wooden bodies that unfold from a carrying case with blades in their arms, moved by silk thread spun with steel hair that the puppeteer keeps on a spool at the wrist. Makers prize Kodama Heartwood above all for joints, a slip of wood from a fallen spirit tree that is only ever given, never cut. Pins, joints, thread and lacquer for mending are sold on Polishers' Street on Tetsuyama. A broken puppet is repaired rather than replaced, so an old puppeteer's puppets are often older than the puppeteer. Karakuri puppeteers will talk about their puppets at length to anyone who stands still, and about their clan's methods not at all.

lore.name: Raiju, the Thunder Beast
lore.info: Raiju is the thunder beast, a wolf of blue-white lightning that comes down out of a storm and goes back up with it. Farmers on the Miyako Plain, woodcutters in the Kurosugi Range and porters on the Fifty Stations Road all know the signs: a cedar split from crown to root, claw marks burned into the bark, a smell like hot iron after the rain. Mothers tell children to sleep on their bellies in a thunderstorm, because a raiju looking for shelter curls up in a sleeper's navel. The beast is not cruel. It is terrified of the storm that carries it and runs blind through fences, walls and anyone standing in the way. Clubs and staves do little to it, and a gale only drives it faster. Fire is what turns it: a bonfire lit in a farmyard or a torch swung in its face will send it bolting the other way. Porters who see lightning walking on the ground get off the road and lie flat until it passes.

lore.name: Ranks and Titles
lore.info: Ranks are carried as titles by samurai: a retainer serves a house or a lord; a captain leads soldiers; a general commands a larger force; an administrator rules a town or district on behalf of the Shogunate. A peasant has no rank but may gain one by rising to a craft guild's mastery, becoming a shrine keeper or winning fame as a warrior. Ranks are held for life unless stripped by judgment or dishonour; a ronin has no rank but the title of their wandering status. An onmyoji holds the rank of diviner or exorcist; a samurai without a house holds no rank but that of masterless.

lore.name: Ranks of the Four Great Houses
lore.info: The four great houses each name their ranks after their own way of war. House Takamori climbs from Retainer to Sworn Sword, Banner Officer and Hatamoto, and its highest swords are called The Regent's Blade. House Kurogane runs from Iron Retainer to Ironclad, Forge Captain and Iron Hatamoto, with The Black Iron Lord's Hand at the top. House Mizuchi ranks its people as a ship would: Deckhand Retainer, Boarding Spear, Ship's Officer, Captain of the River-Dragon and The Admiral's Right Hand. House Hiwada starts its people in the stables as Grooms, then makes them Outriders, Arrow Captains and Banner Riders, and the lord's closest riders are The Sun-Arrow Lord's Hand. The names tell a stranger a good deal: a Kurogane captain has worked the forges, a Hiwada retainer has mucked out horses, and a Mizuchi officer has kept a deck in a storm. Rank does not carry across from one house to another, so a Takamori hatamoto visiting the iron castle is owed courtesy there, not obedience.

lore.name: Ranks of the Hidden Villages
lore.info: The ranks of the hidden villages run in five steps, and Kagegi and Hayate name them alike, each in its own sign. Kagegi has Shadow Apprentice, Shadow Runner, Shadow Captain and Shadow Elite; Hayate has Wind Apprentice, Wind Runner, Gale Captain and Storm Elite. Above them stand the few shinobi trusted to carry the village head's word: The Shadow Head's Hand in the cedar valley, The Wind Head's Hand on the ridges. Apprentices are the youngsters of the training grounds, called genin on the roads, and they move up only by passing the rank exams held among the wires and bells of the Valley of the Rank Exams below Kagegi. Runners take ordinary contracts in teams; captains lead those teams and answer for them at the mission hall; elites take the work that is never written down. Rank is shown by what a shinobi is trusted with rather than by any badge, and an outsider who asks a shinobi's rank is usually told something polite and untrue.

lore.name: Ranks of the Mountain Temple
lore.info: The Mountain Temple Order ranks its people by vow and by years. A Lay Brother keeps the rule without the full vow: carrying water, weeding the herb terraces, sweeping steps and learning the sutras by heart. A Mountain Ascetic has taken the vow and walks the high paths, fasting and standing under the falls. An Exorcist Monk has been taught to drive out possessing spirits with staff, sutra and fire, and is the monk a village sends for when someone starts speaking in another voice. A Temple Abbot keeps one temple, its guests and its fields. The High Abbot's Hand are the monks who carry High Abbot Ryokai's word from the temple of the seven falls to the rest of the range. Senior monks wear strings of green jade prayer beads; the fighting monks wear only hardened cloth guards on their forearms, the one armour the rule allows. The Order takes anyone, and once a newcomer's head is shaved it does not ask what they were before.

lore.name: Ranks of the Road and the Port
lore.info: The ranks of the road and the port are the ones ordinary travellers meet most often. The Post-Road Wardens start their people as Post Riders, who carry the mail between stations in Warden blue, and raise them to Road Guards, who man the barriers and walk the patrols. Station Masters each run one post station; Barrier Captains command a toll barrier and its ledger; The Road Commissioner's Hand carry Road Commissioner Hayashi's orders up and down the highway. The Saikai Merchant Guild runs from Counting-House Runner, a youngster carrying ledgers between floors, to Guild Factor, who buys and sells on the guild's account, then Ledger Keeper, then Master of a Quay, who rules one stretch of the harbour and its dues, and finally Voice of the Guild Council. Guild clerks go about in dark blue coats. A traveller who knows which of these people to bow to, and which to tip, gets through a barrier or a customs shed a good deal faster than one who does not.

lore.name: Revenants of the Mine Shafts
lore.info: The weeping revenants of Tetsuyama are miners' bodies that walk the deep shafts without anything behind their eyes. Miners' Town tells of them in low voices: shapes with lanterns that stand at old bellows and pump them where no forge is lit, guard tunnels nobody has worked in years, and weep at night. The Revenant Shaft is the one every miner names, and none will work it. The families of men who went down and never came up say the strangest thing of all is that a revenant stops and weeps when it hears its old name called. Nobody above ground claims to know what empties a man this way. Swords cut them without slowing them, and curses barely touch them. Old miners say a pick handle or a hammer breaks them better than a blade, and that a priest's prayer does more than either.

lore.name: Rice, Farming and the Peasant
lore.info: Rice is the lifeblood of the isles: it grows in paddies in Miyako Plain and the Mistmarsh, is taxed by the Shogunate, and is the measure of a lord's wealth. A peasant tills his own small plot or works another's fields, paying tax in rice to the Shogunate through the magistrate and to his lord if he lives on the lord's land. A good harvest feeds a family and leaves a surplus to trade; a poor harvest means hunger and borrowing against the next year. Farming is hard, uncertain work; peasants know the weather, the seasons and the land better than any city dweller. The Shogunate's rice tax is the greatest burden on farmers' lives.

lore.name: Rites of the Dead
lore.info: When a person dies, their body is washed and dressed in white, then cremated by the next sunset if the family can pay for it. The ashes are given to the family or scattered in a river; a grave stone is erected at a shrine, where descendants may come to pray. The Veil Court is said to ferry the dead across the boundary between worlds; if a body is not properly cremated and mourned, the spirit may linger as a hungry ghost. Families perform memorial rites on the anniversary of a death, bringing food and flowers to the grave stone. A person who dies away from home has their ashes carried to their family's shrine.

lore.name: Rokurokubi, the Long-Necked Women
lore.info: A rokurokubi is a woman by day whose neck stretches out at night, the head wandering out on a long coil of neck to peer through windows, frighten sleepers and lap the oil from the lamps. Innkeepers on the Fifty Stations Road, the Miyako Plain and the back streets of Saikai say the surest sign is a lamp that was full at bedtime and dry by morning with no one admitting to it. The cruel part of the tale is that most rokurokubi never learn what they become at night. A maid, a wife or a guest wakes tired and stiff and remembers only bad dreams. Startled, the head flees back to its body; cornered, it bites. Folk say a blade at the stretched neck is the surest weapon, and that the creature is harmless again at dawn. Charms and curses slide off a rokurokubi, which is why kind families who suspect one of their own keep the lamps out of her room and the matter out of the magistrate's hearing.

lore.name: Runaway Paper Familiars
lore.info: A paper familiar that has slipped its maker's control is one of the stranger hazards of the Seimei Bureau's district and the Ayakashi Wood. Shikigami constructs of folded paper, crane, hound or warrior, are woken by onmyoji to serve, and most stay at their masters' heels. A few are left behind when an onmyoji dies on the road, or keep carrying out an order long after anyone remembers giving it. They obey the letter of their command and nothing else, so a hound told to guard a gate will guard it against its own master's widow. Clubs crumple them without stopping them, poison does little, and curses do nothing to paper. Townsfolk around Seimei know the plain answers: a bucket of water, a torch, or tearing the talisman pasted on the familiar's back, which turns it into a sheet of paper on the spot. A folded crane flying against the wind is reported to the Bureau, not chased.

lore.name: Sake and Tea
lore.info: Sake is the drink of ceremony, celebration and comfort in the isles: made from rice and water, brewed by specialists, and served warm or cool depending on the season. A cup of sake seals an agreement; three cups drunk together bind sworn brotherhood. Tea is made from leaves grown in mountain valleys and dried, steeped in hot water, and served ceremonially or simply depending on the occasion. A tea master can be as honoured as a swordmaster; the tea ceremony is a meditation on beauty and presence. Tea houses serve tea and small cakes, and are places for quiet talk; sake halls serve sake and loud company.

lore.name: Sake Brewing
lore.info: Sake brewing is winter work in the isles, begun when the rice is in, the air is cold and farm hands are free to hire out to the breweries. Polished rice is washed, steamed, cultured with a mould that turns its starch sweet, and set to ferment in great cedar vats with clean water. The head brewer judges every stage by smell and taste, sleeps beside the vats when they are working, and is paid and guarded like any master craftsman. Breweries stand where the water is good, and the rice of Miyako Plain feeds most of them. The first cask of each season is offered at the local shrine before any is sold, and a fresh cedar ball hung over a brewery's door tells the street that new sake is ready. Cheap sake goes out in gourd flasks to every town market; good sake goes to lords, shrines and the tea houses of the pleasure districts. In the cold north, sailors, miners and hunters drink theirs warm and argue about whose brewery is best.

lore.name: Schooling and Reading
lore.info: Schooling in the isles depends on station and on luck. Samurai children learn letters, poetry, the sword and etiquette in their lord's household or a licensed school, and House Takamori drills its retainers in poetry as hard as in swordwork. Merchant children learn the abacus and the ledger early, and a Saikai counting-house runner can reckon faster than most lords. Village children learn what the temple monks or the headman can spare: enough characters to read a notice, sign a tax register and keep the household accounts. The Shogunate licenses sword schools and the masters who teach in them. The Seimei Bureau takes students at about sixteen and keeps them for years of ink, stars and folding; the Mountain Temple teaches its novices the sutras by heart; the hidden villages teach their own, and say nothing of how. Many commoners never learn to read at all, and pay a letter-writer by the market whenever a letter must be sent or answered.

lore.name: Sea Eagles of the Northern Cliffs
lore.info: Sea eagles are the great white-tailed eagles of the northern coasts, wider across the wings than a man is tall. They nest on the Eagle Cliffs of the Black Stone Coast in the Hyoga Reach and on the headlands of the Mistmarsh Coast, and their screams carry over the surf. A sea eagle takes fish from the water, lambs from the pasture and anything a careless person is carrying that smells of food, including a whole salted fish off a drying rack. Exiles who climb for eggs or feathers go in pairs, one to climb and one to watch the sky, because a nesting eagle attacks climbers with talons and beak. Fishermen gutting on the rocks throw the heads well away from themselves, and shepherds keep their lambs close in spring. A sea eagle that loses its nest to a storm will haunt a fishing village for weeks.

lore.name: Seals and Sealing: The Arts of Binding
lore.info: Sealing is the shinobi's greatest art and the onmyoji's most careful work: binding power, spirits, beasts, or curses into a form that will hold. A seal written poorly is worse than no seal at all, because a broken seal can release what was bound even more powerfully than if there had been no binding. The nine great beasts are sealed by methods so ancient that no one now remembers how they were done; the Vault Wardens spend their lives learning the seals one piece at a time, gradually understanding them through observation and prayer. There are seals written into the land itself, into mountains and lakes, creating safe places where spirits cannot trespass. The most dangerous seals are those written into living things: a cursed spirit bound into a human host, or a beast's power woven into a bearer's bones. These seals are called Birthrights, and they are as likely to tear the bearer apart as to grant them power.

lore.name: Seals and Wards
lore.info: Seals are written by onmyoji on paper or carved into stone, binding spirits, sealing curse wells or preventing entry to forbidden places. A ward is a larger seal, painted or built into the earth around a city or shrine, protecting it from spirits and curses. Wards keep the capital's walls safe and the Bureau's city pristine; a ward can be maintained only by an onmyoji trained in its keeping. Breaking a seal or crossing a ward carries curse and bad fortune; most folk respect them by habit and by genuine fear of the consequences of breaking them. A seal on a person's door means the house is under quarantine or spirit-touched; no one enters without the onmyoji's leave.

lore.name: Seasons and Weather by District
lore.info: The Isles have winter in the north—deep snow in Hinode Hold and Hyoga Reach, demon nights and hard freezing—and autumn-like weather in the south year-round. Spring comes late to the mountains, early to Saikai. The Mistmarsh floods in the summer rains; travel there is dangerous from fifth month to seventh month. Ashfall Blight is always grey and choked with ash-dust; the wind there shifts the ash into drifts like snow. Ayakashi Wood is mist-bound in autumn, hard to navigate; summer there is green and lush. The sea routes are safest from spring through autumn; winter brings storms that close the straits for weeks at a time.

lore.name: Seimei, the Ward City
lore.info: Seimei is the onmyoji city on the Lake of Stars, and across the isles its name means talismans, star-reading and the calendar of lucky days. The whole town lives off the Bureau of Yin and Yang: students and ward-scribes, paper makers and ink grinders, almanac printers, talisman stalls, and the lake boatmen who bring in pilgrims and merchants. Seimei people are thought clever, exact and a little cold, and the joke elsewhere is that a Seimei man consults the calendar before he sneezes. Pilgrims come to buy luck before weddings, journeys and lawsuits, and on the Star Festival wishes on paper strips hang from bamboo along Moonview Bridge while lanterns float on the lake. At the Lake Gate Post every arriving traveller is checked for curses with a paper charm, and the polite thing is to hold still and let the clerk look. A visitor must never touch, mark or step over the carved stones of the ward wall or the seal posts at the crossings, and should not buy a cheap charm in a back lane and then complain to the Bureau when it fails. After dark the sensible keep to the lit avenues and stay out of Haunted Teahouse Lane.

lore.name: Shikigami: Summoned Servants
lore.info: Shikigami are spirits bound by onmyoji into paper forms that wake to serve. A shikigami is not alive but not quite dead; it is will made into shape for the time it remains sealed. Onmyoji draw the seal into paper or fabric, and the spirit answers: sometimes flying, sometimes taking humanoid form, sometimes remaining as floating paper. A shikigami stays bound only as long as the onmyoji's will holds it, and stronger shikigami demand more strength to keep sealed. The oldest shikigami are barely servants at all—they are spirits so powerful that the binding is more a negotiation than a command. Some shikigami have been in service for centuries, passed from master to student, and they have developed personalities and preferences. A shikigami that grows fond of its master might stay bound longer than commanded; a shikigami that grows angry might strain the seal until it breaks.

lore.name: Ships and the Sea
lore.info: The isles are surrounded by water; a ship is the fastest way to travel long distances. Merchant ships are big and slow, built to carry cargo; military ships are smaller and swift, built for speed and manoeuvre. The Mizuchi fleet dominates the straits; sailors of Mizuchi ships are disciplined and well-paid. A ship captain has absolute authority over his crew and his ship; a mutiny at sea is so serious that the mutineers will be hanged if the ship reaches port. Fishing boats work the shallows year-round; a fisherman's catch is often bartered rather than sold for Mon. Shipwrights work in every harbour; a new ship is a major investment and takes months to build.

lore.name: Shirokawa, the Exiles' Town
lore.info: Shirokawa is the exiles' town on the sheltered shore of the Hyoga Reach, and to the south it is the end of the world, the place the realm sends people it wants to forget. Its trades are fish, seal skins and oil, whale oil from the Whaling Station, driftwood, a little smuggling, and the ferry across the White Strait, which costs about thirty Mon when the floes let it run. Shirokawa people are hard, proud and loyal to one another; the south calls them traitors and criminals, and they answer that the south never came to ask. The town keeps one firm custom: nobody asks a newcomer's name, crime or past, and a stranger who asks such things of others is soon drinking alone. Quarrels go to the Exiles' Hall and are settled over drink. The town's great night is the Whale Moon, when every exile who can row goes out after the whales. A visitor should not wander up the Road to the Vaults past the warning poles, should not pick a fight with the Warden hunters who watch the Ice Pier, and should never boast of a southern lord's favour. Those who share their fire and their catch are remembered well.

lore.name: Shrines and the Kami
lore.info: Shrines stand in every town, village and crossroads, tended by a keeper or a priest who performs daily rites to the kami—spirits of place, weather, ancestors and elemental forces. Travellers pray at shrines before long journeys; farmers pray for rain and good harvests; households keep small shrines to their ancestors. A shrine keeper is often the town's oldest or wisest person, consulted on matters of tradition and right action. Large shrines have more priests and hold festivals; the Temple of Safe Voyages in Saikai is massive and wealthy from merchants' donations.

lore.name: Snow Monkeys of the North
lore.info: Snow monkeys are the red-faced monkeys of the snow country in Hinode Hold and the Hyoga Reach. Their troops winter around hot springs, and at Snow Monkey Springs they sit up to their necks in the hottest pools while travellers try to bathe beside them. They are clever, bold and quick: a troop will raid a camp for rice, empty a saddlebag, and steal anything that shines, from a hairpin to a hunter's whetstone. Their screams carry for miles across the snow, and a troop that has spotted a stranger tells the whole valley. Travellers learn to keep packs tied shut and food out of sight, and never to chase a monkey up a slope, because the rest of the troop waits at the top. Trappers at the Snowbound Trading Post consider them harder to catch than foxes and not worth the bother.

lore.name: Soul-Blades: Steel Forged from Living Soul
lore.info: A soul-blade is a sword or spear with a spirit in it, and the spirit has a name its bearer must learn. Called by that name, the blade wakes into a shape of its own and lends a power for a while; learned fully, the name lets the spirit stand beside its bearer and the blade become its true form for one terrible exchange. Soul-blades wake in two stages over a lifetime of practice, and drawing on one spends the bearer's strength. Some have carried the same name for generations, passed from master to student; others wake with one bearer and sleep again when that bearer dies. Smiths and sword-masters argue over where the spirits come from, and the honest ones admit they do not know. A blade with a spirit is never quite sure where it ends and its bearer begins.

lore.name: Spirits of Element and Season
lore.info: Spirits of the five elements—Ember Sprite of fire, Frost Spirit of ice, Gale Spirit of wind, River Serpent of water, and stones that wake to life as guardians—are not yokai born of the land but the land's own will given form. They serve no court and follow no law but the cycle: fire spirits rage in summer, frost spirits dance in winter, wind spirits move where they please. Most are not intelligent in human ways; they are forces that learned to speak. Onmyoji can bind element spirits to serve, but the binding is temporary and costs much. The strong element spirits—a full-grown Gale Spirit or an ancient River Serpent—are beings of such power that even the sealed beasts notice them. They are rarer than great yokai, and sightings of them are marked in histories and remembered for centuries.

lore.name: Stages of the Traditions
lore.info: Every tradition in the isles has three thresholds past the first: a choice of road at the tenth year of practice, the road's elder form at the thirtieth, and an apex at the fiftieth that both roads reach. Shinobi: Shadow of the Village or Masterless Shade, then Village Elder or Ghost of the Range, then The Unseen Hand; Samurai: Sword of the House or Sword of the Realm, then House Champion or Shogunate General, then The Undrawn Blade; Ronin: Wandering Saint or Killing Edge, then The Road's Mercy or The Road's Terror, then The Last Ronin; Veil Officer: Ranked Officer or Renegade of the Veil, then Division Commander or Exile King, then Keeper of the Gate; Half-Yokai: Human Heart or Yokai Heart, then Bridge of Two Worlds or Lord of the Wood, then The Twice-Born; Onmyoji: Court Diviner or Wild Exorcist, then Master of the Bureau or Mountain Saint, then The One Who Reads Heaven; Breath Hunter: Keeper of the Wall or Lone Hunter, then Warden of the Wall or Demon's Bane, then Sunrise Incarnate; Curse-Bearer: Curse Mastered or Curse Embraced, then Curse-Breaker or Grudge Sovereign, then The One Who Ended It. A Named Soul-Blade keeps its own count: its name learned at the fifteenth year, its spirit awakened at the thirty-fifth.

lore.name: Stone Guardians of Gate and Tomb
lore.info: Stone guardians are the carved lions, dogs and warriors that stand at old temple gates, tombs and shrines, woken by seals so old that nobody living knows the words. In the Kurosugi Range, on Tetsuyama and around Seimei folk treat any carved figure with a seal on its base as possibly awake. A guardian defends its gate, its tomb or its shrine and nothing else. It will not chase anyone beyond the ground it keeps, it cannot be bribed or persuaded, and it does not tire. Blades and arrows chip it without stopping it, and earth-arts barely scratch it. What wears it down is what wears down all stone: wind, grit and time. Pilgrims who stray past one bow, back away slowly and come in by another path. Grave robbers who try to fight one are found at the threshold the next morning, and the guardian is found exactly where it always stood.

lore.name: Straw Dolls of the Hour of the Ox
lore.info: Straw dolls are the commonest tool of a private curse: an effigy of the enemy, nailed to a sacred tree at the hour of the ox, the dead middle of the night, by someone in white with an iron hammer. Folk say the curse fails if the curser is seen, which is why the work is done alone and late. The Weeping Cedar in the Ashfall Blight bristles with dolls and nails, old ones rusted black and a few still bright. Sometimes a doll comes down from the tree and walks, stiff-legged, to finish what it was nailed up for. Such a doll has been met in the Ashfall Blight, the Ayakashi Wood and the villages of the Miyako Plain. Arrows and spear points do little to packed straw, and curse-breaking barely touches it. A blade cuts it apart, and it burns like a field after harvest, so farmers who find straw underfoot where no straw should be reach for a lamp before a sword.

lore.name: Sun Peak of the Breath
lore.info: Sun Peak rises behind the ascetics' peak into air so thin the first hundred steps leave a hunter gasping, which is the mountain's first lesson. A cook keeps a small blue fire at the first landing and a warden counts climbers' steps; above them stands a boulder the size of a house, scored with the marks of every hunter who tried to cut it in one breath, and above that the Dark Side, a slope the sun never reaches where the mountain's own demons test the hunters who come to be tested. The mountain has one law: no kill before dawn. The demons know it and use it, and a hunter who breaks it is hunted by name thereafter. Anyone the gate admitted may climb, eat at the cook's fire, and try the boulder; the keeper says it is slightly smaller than it was. Breath Hunters come here for the whole breath: drills until the lungs change, the boulder cut in one breath, and a night on the Dark Side.

lore.name: Sword Polishing and Fittings
lore.info: Sword polishing is the second half of a blade's making, and on Tetsuyama it is done on Polishers' Street below the forges of Hibana. A polisher spends weeks on one sword, kneeling at a low bench in an open-fronted shop and working through a series of whetstones from coarse to fine until the temper line shows clean and the steel carries no scratch the eye can find. The street is quiet enough that the scrape of steel on stone is the loudest sound in it. Scabbard-makers, grip-wrappers and guard-makers belong to the same guild and work near by, so a blade leaves the street dressed as well as sharpened. The shops also sell raw lacquer for scabbards and armour, and the pins, joints and silk thread that puppeteers use for repairs. Master Polisher Togi is the best known of the masters, a fussy man who checks his apprentice's every stroke under the lamp. Polishers like to say that a smith can make a good blade but only a polisher can show anyone that it is good.

lore.name: Swordsmithing at Hibana
lore.info: Swordsmithing at Hibana begins with tamahagane, the rough jewel steel that comes out of the forge town's furnaces in lumps, and ends in the guild's inspection room. A master works with a small team: apprentices pump the bellows and swing the heavy hammers while the master turns, folds and draws out the steel. The blade is coated in clay, thick on the back and thin at the edge, and quenched in the hot springs below Forge Row, which is what gives it its temper line. Masters choose their customers. Each forge door carries its master's crest, buyers wait on the benches outside to be accepted or sent away, and some lodge for weeks at the Hot Spring Inn until a commission is done. Finished blades go down to the polishers and then to the Forge Guild Hall, where examiners turn them in daylight and stamp the guild mark on those that pass. A guild-stamped katana sells for about 30 Mon and one from a named master for about 90. Smiths rise from Forge Apprentice to Journeyman Smith and Master Smith, and a very few become Blade Wakers.

lore.name: Sworn Brotherhood
lore.info: Sworn brothers or sisters are soldiers or companions who take an oath together to stand by each other unto death, sealing it with sake drunk from the same cup and blood mixed together. A sworn-brother bond is not a marriage but a vow to shield each other in battle, avenge each other if one falls, and share what they have. A sworn brother's death is a debt paid only in blood or in living honourably enough that the dead one's name is remembered. The rituals are performed in shrines or at the side of the road; a witnessed oath is valid everywhere in the isles.

lore.name: Tanuki Tricksters and Shape-Stealers
lore.info: Tanuki are yokai of disguise and illusion, cousins to the foxes but less honorable and more mercenary. Where a fox will eat your heart for love or hate, a tanuki will sell you a dream and call it a bargain. They live in groves and hollows across the isles, mostly in Ayakashi Wood where their thievery is considered business. A tanuki can take any shape it sees, and it will steal not just things but faces, voices, entire lives if the price is right. Tanuki respect cleverness above all else, and their courts are built on gambling and deals and debts that stretch across centuries.

lore.name: Tasogare, the City of Farewells
lore.info: Tasogare is the shrine city on the Veilgate cliffs, and across the isles it is where people go to say goodbye. Most of its living comes from grief: pilgrims' lodgings, paper lanterns with the names of the dead written on them, incense, prayers for hire, grave goods, and the coaches that bring mourners up from Kagegi Village. Tasogare folk are gentle, quiet and patient with weeping strangers, and other towns find them unsettling because they speak of the dead as if they had only gone into the next room. The city's great days are Obon at Tasogare, when lanterns float out from the cliffs for three nights to guide the dead home. A visitor should speak softly on the shrine streets, let the lantern-sellers write a name rather than scrawling it themselves, and keep well back from the edge at the great pale torii, which is not a gate for the living. Nobody should mock the black-coated officers of the Veil Court, pick up a white mask from the shore below the cliffs bare-handed, or call a dead person's name aloud after dark, which the townsfolk say invites an answer.

lore.name: Tea Houses and Roadside Tea
lore.info: Tea houses are where most people in the isles drink their tea, and they come in every grade. At the bottom are roadside benches under an awning, like the Rice-Cake Peddlers' Rest near Oiwake Station, where walkers buy cheap tea and toasted rice cakes and trade news for the price of a cup. Town tea houses serve tea and sweets to merchants making deals and to friends meeting quietly. Some serve one trade: duelists sign each other's books at the Duelists' Teahouse on the post road, translators take work by the hour at the Translators' Tea House in Saikai's Foreigners' Quarter, and off-duty Veil officers drink at the Ferrymen's Rest. The tea houses of Lantern Row belong to the pleasure district and serve music and company along with the tea. Tea reaches the towns as dried leaf or ground powder in sealed jars. Powder whisked in a bowl is the formal way to serve it, and leaf steeped in a pot is the everyday one. A tea house keeper hears more than a priest and repeats less, or soon has no customers.

lore.name: Temples and the Mountain Order
lore.info: Temples are the homes of the Mountain Temple Order: mountain ascetics, exorcist monks and shrine keepers who follow the ancient disciplines. A temple is both a place of worship and a refuge: temples take in the sick, the dying, people fleeing violence, and even sworn killers if they renounce the blade and take the vow. A temple keeps its own law and its own order; the Shogunate respects the temple's sanctuary and does not pursue the hunted into its grounds. The Order's abbots are consulted on matters of spirit and soul; their word on whether a curse is real or a conscience's fancy carries weight even with magistrates.

lore.name: Tengu of Peak and Sky
lore.info: Tengu are yokai of wind and height, shape-shifters who live on the high peaks of Kurosugi and Ayakashi Wood, and who descend to the lower lands only when they please. They are proud and vain, with long noses and turbulent tempers. Some tengu are tiny tricksters who steal sandals and cause travelers to lose the path; the greatest tengu are persons of considerable power who can challenge samurai and win. The Tengu Court in Ayakashi Wood keeps its own law and does not answer to any human authority. Tengu respect martial skill and despise cowardice. A tengu provoked will pursue its enemy for years if necessary, but a tengu properly bested might become an ally. Their feathers are treasured by onmyoji for wards and talismans, which is why the feather plucking stopped centuries ago.

lore.name: The Ages of the Isles
lore.info: The folk of the Asagiri Isles count their history in four ages, though no two storytellers agree where one ends and the next begins. First came the age of the great beasts, when nine of them walked the land and the oldest foxes of the wood were worshipped as gods; it ended when the beasts were bound under seals older than the empire. Then came the age of the emperors and the old capital on the plain that is now the Blight, when the first emperor broke the mountain clans and the great houses rose in his service. That age ended three centuries ago in the last great war, when six houses fought over the throne until the old capital burned. The third age is the age of Miyako, in which the houses still fought one another, as at Sekigane a hundred years ago, but never again for the throne. The fourth age, the old people say, began with the regency, and they expect it to end on the day the old emperor dies.

lore.name: The Army Under the Ice
lore.info: The Frozen Battlefield is a field on the Hyoga Reach where an army stands in its ranks under clear ice, spears raised and banners stiff, and the exiles of Shirokawa have made a whole cycle of stories from it. No house in the south claims the army, and nobody can read the marks on its banners. The common tale says it marched north to carry the war to the Northern Court and was caught by a cold so sudden that the soldiers froze mid-stride with their faces toward the enemy. Another tale, which the exiles naturally prefer, says it was a southern army sent to drive the first exiles off the isle and was punished by the ice for it. Exiles avoid the field and warn newcomers not to stare into the ice, saying that a face looked at too long will be seen again in dreams. Lately travellers have reported a demon of the Northern Court in black armour walking slowly among the frozen ranks, and fewer exiles than ever will go near the place.

lore.name: The Ashfall Blight's War
lore.info: The Ashfall Blight marks where the isles fought their last great war three centuries ago, when the old capital stood on that plain and six great houses fought for the throne. No one remembers what the war was for any more. What remains is ash, craters where lords' palaces burned, broken banners half-buried in grey soil, and wells that filled with curse instead of water as thousands of dying men spilled their grudges into the ground. The new capital, Miyako, was built south after the war; the old palace's ruins stand in the Blight now, untouched by farmer or scholar. The road past them is hurried.

lore.name: The Bells of the Drowned Village
lore.info: The Drowned Village on the Mistmarsh Coast was a fishing village until a great storm took it, and the coast tells its story as a warning about the sea. The tale says the storm came in a single night, that the water rose over the roofs before the people could reach high ground, and that the shrine bell went down still hanging in its frame. At low tide the weed-black ridges of the roofs still show in rows where the streets once ran, and the torii of the Sunken Shrine stands up to its crossbeam in the water. On calm nights the fishermen of Ashiura hear bells ringing under the waves and say it is the drowned calling the hours as they did in life. No net is cast over the village and no boat anchors there; a fish caught in those waters by mistake is thrown back. Some families along the coast still leave rice on their doorsteps on the anniversary of the storm, for kin who never had a grave, and a clapper from the drowned bell is a thing no honest fisherman would keep.

lore.name: The Binding of the Great Beasts
lore.info: The binding of the nine great beasts is the oldest story told in the isles, and nobody tells it the same way twice. In the common version the beasts roamed the land before the empire: the Ember Ox cracking mountains under its hooves, the Drowned Crane bringing floods, the Gale Serpent raising storms, and each of the others a disaster with a shape. The people of that time, whose names are lost, learned to bind the soul-current into seals and set out to cage the beasts one by one. Most were laid under the ice of Hyoga, where the Sealing Vaults stand over them now. Two were never taken there: the mountain folk say one lies under a peak of the Kurosugi Range held by prayer, and the yokai of the wood say another waits high in the Ayakashi Wood. Some of the beasts' power would not stay in their bodies, and the sealers bound it into living people instead, the first hosts. Grandmothers end the tale the same way everywhere: the sealers paid with their lives, and that is why nobody remembers how it was done.

lore.name: The Breath Hunters of Hinode
lore.info: The Breath Hunters of Hinode are the demon-hunting order of the snowy north-east, sworn to kill the demons that come south from the Northern Court. They fight with sun-steel blades and the breathing forms of their schools (Ember, Tide, Gale, Stone, Thunder, Mist, Blossom, Beast), and they hold the fortress of Hinode Hold and the wall below it. Most hunters are orphans of demon raids. The north worships them; the capital forgets them until the Demon Nights come.

lore.name: The Brine Tide
lore.info: The Brine Tide are the smugglers of the east coast: a brotherhood of captains, fishermen and harbour rats who run salt, sake, foreign silver and anything else untaxed through the Mistmarsh channels to Saikai and back. They pay off Mizuchi captains, hire Kirisame guides and settle quarrels at the Drowned Lantern in Ashiura. Coast villages live on their trade. The navy hunts them when the admiral is watching and drinks with them when he is not.

lore.name: The Calendar and Lucky Days
lore.info: The Seimei Bureau reads the stars and the old calendar to determine lucky days and unlucky days: auspicious days for weddings, funerals, travel, trade and war, and days to be avoided for anything important. A lord will not begin a campaign on an unlucky day; a merchant will not launch a ship. Magistrates consult the Bureau's calendar before issuing important judgments. The calendar is ancient, passed down through centuries, and most folk trust it as much as they trust the magistrate. A person born on an unlucky day is said to carry that misfortune their whole life, though a few famous heroes were born on the most unlucky days of all.

lore.name: The Changes of the Otherworld
lore.info: What the Otherworld's masters teach is not a technique but a change, and it changes only a character of the master's own tradition; companions who train beside them gain what watching teaches and nothing more. A Breath Hunter leaves with Sun Peak Forms, a whole breath style. A Veil Officer leaves with True Release, their blade's name spoken and its released form theirs to wear for a scene. A Half-Yokai leaves with Both Bloods Known and a court that treats them as kin. A Shinobi leaves with a Second Style, one Element not their own, in the shinobi idiom. A Samurai leaves with their House Secret Cut; a Ronin with The Masterless School; an Onmyoji with a Shikigami Pact, a true familiar bound by name; a Curse-Bearer with The Curse Turned, the curse working for its bearer at last. Each change opens exactly three techniques and no more, and the isles notice: a house recognises its secret cut, the Court reads a half-yokai's blood, the hidden villages call a second style forbidden. The arcs are a lesson at the Yard, a trial in the quarter and a proving at its deepest place, and the master decides when the change has taken.

lore.name: The Curse-Hunter Brotherhood
lore.info: The Curse-Hunter Brotherhood are sorcerers who turned their craft against curses: they track curses to their makers, break them, and kill the makers when nothing else works. Many are curse-bearers themselves, carrying a family curse or a bonded relic they have mastered rather than been mastered by. They work for fees from anyone, rich or poor, and keep a chapterhouse on the edge of the Blight. People hire them gratefully and are afraid to have them stay the night.

lore.name: The Demon That Walks by Day
lore.info: The Daylight Demon is the one demon of the Northern Court that northern folk say can bear the sun. Where others burn in moments it endures daylight for hours, though sun-steel still cuts it, and hunters of Hinode Hold have found tracks crossing the snow at Daylight Watch Ridge that should have burned at dawn and did not. Travellers on the Frozen Pass of the Long Night have met it walking by day in a dark cloak, and it let hunters go on their way. Stories of it have since come down the Fifty Stations Road and across White Strait from the Hyoga Reach. It avoids fights, does not seem to want blood, and nobody can say what it does want or why it keeps coming south. Poison and ordinary swords do it little harm. The Breath Hunters argue about it at every mess table: some say a demon that holds back is only waiting, others that a demon with a reason is a demon you can talk to.

lore.name: The Drowned Crane Sealed
lore.info: The Drowned Crane is a great beast of black water whose wings once brought floods that drowned whole valleys. It was sealed in the Sealing Vaults before memory, and there its seal lies beneath ice miles thick and stone deeper still. The Crane remembers every drowning it has caused, and if the seal breaks, the wells and rivers of the isles will answer to it first. Its power is water in the form of hunger and weight and the voice of the deep; those who have touched its sealed chamber speak of water that fell upward and stone that wept. It is the second of the nine great beasts, and its seal is held by the Vault Wardens' watchers on the Long Vigil.

lore.name: The Earth Spider Pits and the Old Clans
lore.info: The Earth Spider Pits in the Kurosugi Range are webbed gullies where, the mountain folk say, the old clans of the range made their last stand against the first emperor and lost. The hamlets tell it as the beginning of the realm: the first emperor came with his armies, the clans who had lived in the mountains before the empire would not bow, and they fought from pits and burrows until the last of them were buried there. Their carved stones still lean at the edge of the gullies, smeared with ochre handprints, and the ochre is always fresh though nobody admits to painting it. Hunters from both hidden villages turn back at the edge, and the only trails in are marked with bones and old arrowheads. Old women of the range say the clans' grudge did not die with them and that the pits are no place for the living. Children are warned that the silk roofing the gullies looks like solid earth until the moment it gives way.

lore.name: The Elements and Their Cycle
lore.info: The soul-current flows through the isles in five forms: Earth that holds and binds, Water that flows and drowns, Fire that burns and consumes, Wind that tears and wears, and Void that empties and tears through spirit. These five meet in a cycle that never breaks: Water drowns Fire, Fire eats Wind, Wind wears Earth, Earth dams Water, and all five fear Sunlight, which thins the Void. When two elements meet in the same technique, the bane pairs refuse to work together, but allied pairs—Ember and Earth for magma, Tide and Wind for storm—strengthen each other. A fighter who masters one element can learn another, but a soul can only carry so much force before it tears. The elements meet in the isles as often as the traditions do, making new fighters and stranger powers.

lore.name: The Ember Ox Sealed
lore.info: The Ember Ox is the first of the nine great beasts, a burning ox the size of a hill whose hooves crack mountains and whose breath is magma. It sleeps in a seal beneath the Sealing Vaults, where the stone around it glows red even through the ice. If it ever wakes, the northern lands will burn, and the heat will crack the ice-isle's spine. The sealers who bound it wore forms that let them not feel pain; some say the Ox's own heat is part of what holds it now, burning endlessly in one place instead of crossing the land. The Vault Wardens rotate watchers at its seal-chamber three times a day, because if anyone falls asleep near it, the Ox's dreams sometimes leak through.

lore.name: The Emperor's Illness
lore.info: The puppet emperor grows visibly weaker each season, tended by court physicians who admit openly they do not know the sickness. Some say it is a curse, others say age and the weight of a name without power. The court sets official times when he receives visitors, though he often sleeps through them; only the Dowager Empress and a few intimates see him in private. The isles watch and wait for his death as soldiers wait for battle orders. When he dies, the succession crisis will open fully; until then, the realm holds its breath and pretends the next emperor has not been chosen already.

lore.name: The Empty Moon Hare Sealed
lore.info: The Empty Moon Hare is smallest of the nine great beasts, a hare whose body is an absence, whose footprints are voids that erase everything they touch. It lies sealed deep beneath Hyoga in a chamber that refills with stone as fast as the stone crumbles away, in a cycle that will continue until the world ends. The Hare does not grow restless; it simply is, erasing slowly, eternally. What terrifies the Vault Wardens most is not that the hare might escape, but that if the seal fails, the void it carries will spread like an illness. It is the fifth of the nine, and some sealers believe it is already dead, and only the seal keeps the void from leaking through.

lore.name: The Empty Throne
lore.info: When the emperor dies, the throne becomes empty: no one sits upon it, no one writes law in its name. The succession crisis fills that emptiness with three claimants and every house positioning itself. The Shogunate continues to rule in the dead emperor's name until the succession is settled; magistrates still enforce the law, toll barriers still stand, but everyone knows that the legitimacy that backed the law is gone. The isles have faced an empty throne before, in the last great war, and what came of it was ash and curse wells. Fear of another war and a desperate hope for peace drive the politics of the succession.

lore.name: The Fallen Gate of the Old Capital
lore.info: The Ruins of the Old Capital are the broken walls and fallen gates of a city older than Miyako, half buried in ash in the Ashfall Blight, and the isles know them mostly through song. Blind biwa monks sing the city's fall in long verses: the six houses fighting street by street for the throne, the palace burning with its banners, and a great gate brought down across the main avenue, where it still lies face down from wall to wall. Common folk call it the Fallen Gate and say that whoever lies on it at night hears the war still being fought underneath. The grey pilgrims walk out from Haibara to lay offerings at the gate and pray for the old city's dead, and curse-hunters walk beside them for their safety. Farmers and scholars alike leave the ruins alone, for the tale says that anything carried out of the old capital draws the grudge fog after it. Travellers who must pass keep to the old paving, stay out of the roofless palace, and do not raise their voices inside the walls.

lore.name: The Far Shore, the Dead's Side
lore.info: The Far Shore is the Veil seen from the other side: a grey tide that never turns, a shingle landing with a ferryman who counts the living, a field of standing stones cut with the names of the ferried where the unferried wait and ask for names, the Court of the Dead where clerks older than the isles keep black ledgers, and a drowned causeway at the end of which a magistrate judges the living by laws repealed a thousand years ago. The living are tolerated here at a price: a memory, paid at the Court's toll door and written down. Refuse it and the Court remembers. Anyone the gate admitted may trade with the dead clerks, read the stones to the waiting, or walk the causeway for what the ferrymen could not carry. Veil Officers come here to hear their blade's true name and meet its spirit among the stones; Curse-Bearers come to meet the one who cursed them, who is very often a clerk.

lore.name: The Fifty Stations Road
lore.info: The Fifty Stations Road is the great highway of the isles, a chain of post stations a day's walk apart that joins Saikai Free Port, the Ashfall Blight, Miyako Plain and the Mistmarsh Coast, with Oiwake Station at its great junction and a ferry across the Ember Strait to Tetsuyama. It is kept by the Post-Road Wardens under the Shogunate's charter: inns, stables, toll barriers and watchtowers manned to keep the road safe for merchants and mail. The road is the isles' spine; armies march it, caravans cross it, and travellers treat it as the one safe path from one end of the realm to another. Its order is sacred: a fight on the road is a crime against the Shogunate itself, and bandits who work it answer to the Wardens.

lore.name: The Five Sanctums of the Elements
lore.info: Five nature worlds share one region behind the Element shrines: a cave of warm stone under a standing stone, a still black pool under mist, an ash field around a crack that breathes heat, a ledge over a bottomless drop where a gale lives in the air, and a hall where grey threads converge on a point the eye slides off. Five stairs part at a moss-roofed hut whose hermit tells each visitor which stair their Element will suffer them on; the stairs rearrange themselves, and the wrong one walks a day and arrives back at the hut. Each Sanctum is kept by what its Element made, and each keeper is a trial before it is a foe: stone forgives no fire, the pool answers whatever is thrown in, the furnace takes poured water as an insult, the gale puts the fallen back on the ledge humiliated, and the thing in the void hall eats attention. Those of an Element cross to their own Sanctum; any Shinobi may cross to any, and a Shinobi who trains in a Sanctum not their own learns a second Element's style, which the hidden villages forbid.

lore.name: The Foreigners' Quarter
lore.info: Saikai's Foreigners' Quarter is where traders from beyond the isles keep warehouses, maintain ships and live in compounds surrounded by high walls. Foreigners are permitted to trade but not to own land or intermarry; a foreigner who takes an island wife may stay but cannot bring her into the Quarter and cannot return to the foreign lands. The Quarter has its own small shrine, foreign-style bathhouses and food cooked in foreign ways. Harbour guards keep watch to prevent goods leaving the isles without the merchant guild's approval, and to ensure no foreign spy makes contact with the local population.

lore.name: The Fox Court
lore.info: The Fox Court is the court of fox spirits in the Ayakashi Wood, ruled by a nine-tailed lady who has watched three dynasties rise and fall. Its foxes are tricksters, shrine messengers, lovers of humans and keepers of debts, and they move among people in borrowed shapes. The Court trades in favours and promises and never forgets either. Villages near the wood leave rice at fox shrines; travellers who eat fox food and break fox promises are seldom seen again.

lore.name: The Free Port Town of Saikai
lore.info: Saikai is known across the isles as the town where anything can be bought and nobody asks which lord a buyer serves. Its trade is the sea: foreign silver and cargo off the square-sailed ships, salt and fish from the coast, swords for hire at the Ronin Hiring Hall, and loans from guild clerks who write down half the realm's debts. Saikai folk are quick, cheerful and hard to cheat, and the rest of the isles says they would sell their grandmother's ashes if the price were fair. A deal struck in Saikai is written down and witnessed, because the port trusts paper more than oaths. Its great night is the Night of the Hundred Ships, when the trading fleet is lit with lanterns and blessed by the bell of the Temple of Safe Voyages. A visitor should pay anchor fees and harbour dues without argument, keep a sword sheathed on the quays, and never borrow from a Lantern Row debt book that cannot be repaid. Above all, nobody should say on the quays that the regent's law runs in Saikai; the port is proud that it does not.

lore.name: The Gale Serpent Sealed
lore.info: The Gale Serpent is a serpent of living wind whose coils once created storms that lasted seasons. It is sealed in the Sealing Vaults beneath layers of stone and binding-seals that whisper constantly with the sound of wind held still. If the Serpent ever escaped, the entire northern reach would be in storm. What makes it most dangerous is that it does not sleep like the other beasts: it thrashes slowly inside its seal, testing the edges, learning them. The Vault Wardens say that each year, the Serpent tests the seal at one new place, and each year they must reinforce it. It is the fourth of the nine, and it remembers what it wants to break.

lore.name: The Gibbets of Pirate Graves Reef
lore.info: Pirate Graves Reef is the wreck-strewn reef off the western cape beyond Saikai, and the port tells its history with a certain pride. In the old days, the tale goes, pirates preyed on every ship that came in from the open sea, and those the port caught were hanged in chains on Gibbet Rock so that every incoming crew would see them before it saw the harbour. The rusted chains still knock against the iron post in the wind. The reef is the worst water on that coast: fog lies on it most mornings, and at low tide the ribs of old ships show among the rocks. Saikai fishermen say the hanged pirates still keep watch for ships to take, and the fishing boats give the whole reef a wide berth. A sailor who loses something overboard near the reef does not go in after it, and nobody in Saikai will wear or sell anything salvaged from the wrecks.

lore.name: The Grave Mounds of Sekigane
lore.info: The Old Battlefield of Sekigane is a field of grave mounds on Miyako Plain where two houses fought a great battle a century ago. The plain still argues over which side had the right of it, and families who sent sons to either army tell the story differently, so innkeepers on the plain learn not to ask. Everyone agrees that the dead were buried where they fell, too many to carry home, each mound topped with a stone. Rusted armour and broken blades still work up out of the ground after heavy rain, and farmers say Sekigane is ploughing itself. Nobody farms the field, and travellers cross it by day and quickly. Skirmishes flared over the same ground for long after the great battle, and some old foot soldiers of the plain fought there in their youth. Grave robbers dig the mounds for old swords, and the plain despises them for it, because a blade taken from a grave is said to carry its dead owner's quarrel to whoever wears it next. Children dare one another to touch the stone on the Great Mound, and few do.

lore.name: The Great Temples: Haibara's Vow and the Mountain Shrine
lore.info: Haibara's Vow Temple sits in Ashfall Blight and exists for one purpose: to witness and mark binding vows. Any person—criminal, saint, curse-bearer, traitor—can come to Haibara and make an oath that will bind their soul until they die. The temple does not judge the oath, only marks it. Some say the temple's ground is so thick with sworn oaths that it has become sacred by weight of promises. The Mountain Temple Order's great temple in the Kurosugi Range is older and quieter: its monks chant the sutras every day without fail, and pilgrims come from across the isles to rest there. Many of them never leave, choosing to stay and pray rather than return to the world.

lore.name: The Grudge Centipede Sealed
lore.info: The Grudge Centipede is the most unusual of the nine great beasts, a creature of iron and living grudge that mountain folk say lies coiled under one of the Kurosugi peaks, held by prayer rather than by the Vaults. The tales say the Centipede's seal is not stone or magic but prayer, though nobody agrees whose prayer or where. If that prayer ever stopped, the Centipede would wake and carry the hatred of centuries out into the world. Unlike the others, it is not a force of nature but a force of will, and it hears every grudge in the isles.

lore.name: The Grudge Well Sorcerers
lore.info: The Grudge Well Sorcerers draw power from the curse wells of the Ashfall Blight, where centuries of grudges have pooled into something a skilled hand can bottle. They brew curses to order, bind cursed relics, and sell both through Saikai's black market to anyone who can pay: a widow wanting a husband's killer dead, a lord wanting a rival's heir sickly. The Blight's few villages pay them to keep the wells quiet. Everyone else calls them poisoners of the soul.

lore.name: The Grudge-Born
lore.info: Not every oni was born one. In the isles a person who carries one feeling too long, sorrow that never ends, shame that is never answered, envy of the one who stood first, can wake one morning with horns. These are the Grudge-Born. Each keeps a fragment of who they were and is held to the world by a single want tied to how they fell: to see someone again, to hear a confession, to win once, to finish one task. They never say what it is, and most no longer know the words for it. Priests teach that a Grudge-Born can be laid to rest three ways: cut down, which takes a hard fight and leaves nothing; given what it wants, when it unbinds and leaves behind one object from its life; or deceived into believing it has it, when it still unbinds, but the object it leaves is cracked, as hollow as the lie. Learning the want means learning the life: the people who knew them, the places they fell, the records of what was done to them.

lore.name: The Half-Yokai Refuge
lore.info: The Half-Yokai Refuge is a hidden village deep in the Ayakashi Wood where the two-blooded live: children of humans and foxes, tengu, oni, kappa, snow-women and stranger things, who are hunted or shunned everywhere else. The Refuge takes in anyone with yokai blood, teaches them to live with what they are, and defends itself fiercely. Neither the Fox nor the Tengu Court owns it, though both claim to protect it. Few humans know the way in.

lore.name: The Hidden Court of the Yokai
lore.info: The Hidden Court is the yokai country as the yokai keep it: an arch of living branches hung with lanterns, a long walk under old trees where the masked promenade and buy lanterns for favours instead of coin, a hall of roots where the courtiers sit in session under their own law, and a tree so old its hollow trunk is a country, with something crowned in its deepest chamber. The Court's one law for guests is plain: steel drawn in the Court Proper without a declared challenge is the worst manners it knows, and it answers bad manners with forgotten favours and darkened lanterns, never with a barred gate. A challenge answered without a cut earns a favour from the Favour Table. Half-Yokai are read aloud here and learn their other parent's kind; they come to walk the Lantern Walk in full form and answer a challenge as kin. Onmyoji come to bind a court spirit by its true name, which the Court permits because it has never been done politely.

lore.name: The Hidden Villages' Public Face
lore.info: To ordinary folk, Kagegi and Hayate villages are small mountain settlements where skilled hunters and guides live. Merchants hire guides from the villages to cross the range safely; the range routes are steep, misty and easy to get lost in. The villages supply shinobi to the great houses only through intermediaries—a merchant family or a lord's steward—so that the houses cannot say they bought assassins directly and the villages keep their independence. The villages themselves are said to be hidebound, ruled by councils of elders, strict about their ways. In truth, the villages' secret business is never discussed with outsiders.

lore.name: The Hired Blade
lore.info: Not every blade in the isles is sworn. A ronin, a shinobi between contracts, an onmyoji with debts or any free hand can ask a faction's officers for work at its seat and be hired for a contract: the same jobs the sworn run, paid in Mon on completion and remembered as goodwill, never counted as merit and never leading to a rank. Hired steel owes no oath, and the custom of the isles is plain about it: a hired blade who works for one house this season and its rival the next is a mercenary, not a traitor; the rival's officers may grow cold, but nobody is branded for it. Treason is the sworn's crime alone: only a character who has taken a faction's oath and then serves its rival against it builds exposure, and only they can be caught and named Turncoat. Many hired blades swear in the end, to the house that paid best or treated them well; a faction's officers remember who worked for them before.

lore.name: The Hundred Blades' Terraces
lore.info: The Hundred Blades are a hundred terraces of swept stone climbing a cliff behind the Shrine of the Fallen Feather. Every visitor lays their sword on the first terrace's flat stone for the keeper to read before a step is taken up, and the swords of those who never came back hang on the wall there, most of them bright. Halfway up an armourer turns a whetstone the size of a millwheel and a duellist who died on the terraces offers bouts to anyone who looks bored; at the top the sword saints give their last lesson, guarded by a student who won a hundred bouts and refused it. The terraces' one law: no cut outside a declared bout. A bout is declared, refereed, and ended by a cut, a draw or a disarm alike. Anyone the gate admitted may climb, fight by the rules, and have a blade whetted against the school it should fear. Samurai come here for the cut their house kept from them; Ronin for the school with no name that answers every school.

lore.name: The Hundred-Duel Circuit
lore.info: The Hundred-Duel Circuit is the brotherhood of wandering duelists who travel the post road seeking a hundred duels: one at each of the Fifty Stations, there and back. Duelists keep a book of their fights signed by each opponent, and a duelist who completes the hundred is honoured at every dojo in the isles. The Circuit has rules (no duel without consent, no fight in a station's yard) and a Book-Keeper who keeps the record of every duelist alive and dead. The Post-Road Wardens hate the Circuit; the crowds love it.

lore.name: The Hyoga Exiles
lore.info: The Hyoga Exiles are the people the isles sent away: political prisoners, disgraced samurai, deserted Veil officers and beast hosts who escaped the Wardens, living in three fishing towns on the ice isle's south shore. They fish, hunt seals and smuggle, and they owe nothing to the regent who exiled them. Exiles are hard, proud and loyal to each other. The south has forgotten them; the Vault Wardens, whose fortress they live beside, have not.

lore.name: The Imperial Court
lore.info: The Imperial Court is the emperor's own household: the old noble families, priests of the sun rites, poets, ladies-in-waiting and keepers of the regalia who live within the palace walls and have no swords and no armies. They hold the one thing the Shogunate cannot make: legitimacy. Every title, every house's right to its lands and every regency was granted with an imperial brush. The people bow to the court's processions and know nothing of what happens inside. The Shogunate pays the court's bills and expects it to stay ornamental.

lore.name: The Isles' Techniques
lore.info: The isles teach that every art is a ladder and every master once stood on its first rung. A student learns the forms of their school, rung by rung; a disciple who has climbed far enough makes forms of their own, and the schools record them under the maker's name. Two students of different traditions who learn to strike as one are rarer and better loved in the songs. And once in a life, sometimes in a youth's first desperate fight, sometimes in an old master's last, a fighter reaches for something no school taught them: their Awakened Art, theirs alone, which the isles will remember with their name. Elements meet in the same way: fire and earth make magma, water and wind a storm, and water simply puts the fire out.

lore.name: The Kirisame Clan
lore.info: The Kirisame Clan are the marsh shinobi of the Mistmarsh Coast, belonging to neither village: rain-callers and poisoners who live in stilt houses among the reeds and know every channel the fog hides. They hire out as smugglers' guides and as assassins whose victims die of a fever three days later. The marsh folk pay them in rice and silence. The Mizuchi navy has tried to burn them out three times and lost ships each time.

lore.name: The Lairs of the Isles
lore.info: Hunters, ronin and shrine-sworn speak of the isles' lairs: the hostile places a named thing holds, from the kappa fords and the smugglers' caves to the frozen battlefield of the demon court. A band that works a lair runs it at one of three lengths, asked for at the mouth ("a quick run", "a full run", "a long hunt"), else the lair's own: a Quick run is one area, the boss its finale; a Full run every area in order; a Long hunt plays each area as two or three beats with a mid-run objective. A cleared lair lies quiet for a season, then something new holds it, and once the named boss has fallen its successor keeps the deep chamber. What a boss held comes out in the crafting steps everyone knows: Plain, Fine, Superior, Master-made, Named. The Hunter's Tally counts clears; the hunters' halls name a band Lair Hunter at 100, Veteran Hunter at 300, Lair Breaker at 700 and Legend of the Lairs at 1500, and treat it so.

lore.name: The Lanterns of Ghost Pine Hill
lore.info: Ghost Pine Hill is the stretch of the Fifty Stations Road where the highway sinks into a cutting between earth walls, and it holds the best-known ghost stories on the road. Station masters warn that lanterns float along the cutting at night with no one carrying them, and that a traveller who follows one forgets where they were going and is found by the road at dawn. The road's other tale is of a pilgrim in grey robes and a deep straw hat who walks the cutting at dusk, asking the way to a shrine that burned down a century ago; the advice told at every inn is to answer nothing, keep walking and never look under the hat. The tiny shrine on the hilltop is abandoned, its bell cord rotted through, and nobody has ever rebuilt it. Post riders who must pass after dark ride hard and keep their eyes on the road. Most travellers simply time their day so that the hill is behind them before the light goes.

lore.name: The Long Dark of the Northern Winter
lore.info: The northern winter is mostly darkness. In Hinode Hold the days shrink to a few grey hours around noon, and across White Strait in the Hyoga Reach the sun barely clears the ice for weeks at a time. People there live by lamplight: the whale oil rendered at the Whaling Station burns all winter in the lamps of Shirokawa, and a family that runs out of oil runs out of light. Cold is the other enemy. Breath freezes on scarves, iron sticks to bare skin, and the Frozen Pass of the Long Night stays frozen nine months of the year. Travellers wait out storms by any stone wall and fire they can find rather than push on, because a blizzard can come without warning and the snow fills tracks within the hour. Northerners stack firewood to the eaves by autumn, and they reckon a neighbour's wealth by the height of that stack.

lore.name: The Long Night
lore.info: The Long Night is what northern folk call the deepest winter, when the days are shortest and the demons of the Northern Court come south to test the Long Night Wall. The Breath Hunters of Hinode stand the wall every year, stockpiling supplies and readying their sun-steel; the worst of those nights are the Demon Nights, when every hunter, recruit and orphan stands the wall till dawn. Ordinary folk speak of it with fear: villages burned, travellers lost in the dark, demons that ordinary steel will not kill. The oldest tales warn of a winter when the Long Night will not end and the demon lord himself marches south. The capital hears these stories as rumours and thanks the hunters that the threat stays far from Miyako's walls.

lore.name: The Long Night Wall and Demon Burning
lore.info: The Long Night Wall at Hinode Hold is built of stones so thick and black that sunlight seems to vanish into them. It marks the boundary where the breath hunters halt their burning each spring; beyond it lie the deep valleys where demons nest during winter. Every spring, when the darkness breaks, the hunters go north with torches and breath-forms blazing, burning out the demon warrens and filling the valleys with smoke and fire. By autumn the demons have returned, and the cycle begins again. The Wall itself has become a symbol: to hold the Wall is to hold the line between civilization and the wild north. Hunters who die defending it are marked in the fortress's honor roll, and their names are spoken at every warming.

lore.name: The Long War With the North
lore.info: The north of the isles has been at war with the Northern Court for as long as anyone has kept records, and the folk of Hinode Hold tell its history as a list of winters. In the oldest tales the demons came south every long night with nothing to stop them, and whole valleys were emptied. The hunters' order began, the Hold says, with orphans of those raids who learned to breathe the soul-current and found that sunlight held in steel burned what ordinary blades could not. They built their fortress facing the sunrise and then the Long Night Wall across the neck of the land, and since then they have burned out the demon nests every spring and stood the wall every winter. The raids have never stopped, only shrunk; Kitamura burned in the most recent of them. Northern families date their lives by the Demon Nights: a child born two Nights after the bad one, a marriage made the year the wall held without a death.

lore.name: The Lotus Ward
lore.info: The Lotus Ward is the faction around Princess Ayame, the Dowager Empress's ward, a young woman of nineteen descended from an old imperial branch line. She is the claimant with the best blood, the gentlest manner and no army. Her cause has drawn court ladies, temple abbots, the Hiwada riders and the village elders of the plain, because she has promised to halve the rice tax and dissolve the Shogunate. Her followers wear a white lotus. The houses think her a puppet; the Dowager thinks her the last chance the isles have to be ruled rather than owned.

lore.name: The Masked Hungry Dead
lore.info: Some of the dead refuse the Veil Court's ferry to rest, clinging to hunger instead of accepting peace.
